Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\khair\.claude\skills\call-another-llm

<purpose>
Send a prompt to another LLM agent and get its response saved to a file.
Two separate scripts, one per LLM. Each runs the CLI in non-interactive mode and writes the raw response to tmp/llm-responses/.
</purpose>

<constraints>
- Each script runs the target LLM in non-interactive mode with auto-approve. Codex specifically runs in YOLO mode (`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`): unsandboxed with full filesystem/network access, so it can implement changes, run tests, and reach the TEST database.
- Fail fast if the target CLI is not installed or returns a non-zero exit code.
- Output files contain only the raw response — no metadata.
- All output goes to `tmp/llm-responses/` with the pattern `<llm>-<label>-<timestamp>.md`.
</constraints>

<scripts>
- `scripts/call_codex.py` — calls Codex CLI
- `scripts/call_claude.py` — calls Claude Code CLI
</scripts>

<inputs>

**All scripts share:**
  - positional: `prompt` (required, except when using `--list-models`)
  - `--label`: optional label for the output filename (default: llm name)

**Codex-specific flags (`call_codex.py`):**
  - `-m` / `--model`: model to use (known model: `gpt-5.6-sol`; any string accepted)
  - `--effort`: reasoning effort level — `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `ultra` (`ultra` is heavy on usage but most capable)
  - `--list-models`: print known models, the current default, and valid effort levels, then exit

When `--model` is omitted, Codex uses the default from `~/.codex/config.toml`.
When `--effort` is omitted, Codex uses the effort configured in `config.toml` (default: `high`).
</inputs>

<workflow>
1. If the user has not specified which LLM to call, use the AskUser tool with options (Codex, Claude) to let the user choose. If the user wants both, confirm that before running two parallel calls.
2. Write the prompt to a file first (see prompt-file-methodology below).
3. Run the chosen script(s) passing the file contents: `"$(cat tmp/llm-prompts/{filename})"`.
4. Read the output file path from stdout (OUTPUT_FILE=...).
5. Read the response file to use the result.
</workflow>

<prompt-file-methodology>
Always write prompts to a file before passing to CLI scripts. This makes prompts reviewable,
debuggable, and preservable as an audit trail.

**Directory:** `tmp/llm-prompts/` (create with `mkdir -p` if it doesn't exist)

**File naming:** `{agentname}_{3 random lowercase letters}_{unix timestamp}.txt`
- `agentname` = the agent role or label (e.g. `codex-reviewer`, `claude-summarizer`)
- 3 random lowercase letters for uniqueness
- Unix timestamp in seconds
- Example: `codex-reviewer_xfm_1743926400.txt`

**Steps:**
1. `mkdir -p tmp/llm-prompts`
2. Generate filename: `{agentname}_$(cat /dev/urandom | tr -dc 'a-z' | head -c3)_$(date +%s).txt`
3. Write the full prompt to that file.
4. Pass to CLI: `uv run .../call_codex.py --label "..." "$(cat tmp/llm-prompts/{filename})"`
</prompt-file-methodology>

<examples>
```bash
# List available Codex models and effort levels
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" --list-models

# Codex with default model and effort
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Explain the trade-offs of this approach" --label "review"

# Codex with specific model and effort
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Review this code" -m gpt-5.6-sol --effort high --label "review"
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_codex.py" "Deep analysis of this architecture" -m gpt-5.6-sol --effort ultra --label "deep-review"

# Claude
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/call-another-llm/scripts/call_claude.py" "Summarise this error log" --label "error-summary"
```
</examples>


ARGUMENTS: Use Codex CLI with gpt-5.6-sol at xhigh reasoning to review the design document at C:\Users\khair\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-khair-Code-Projects-fork-superset-windows-arm64\41b65f55-7b51-4cfd-82d1-d1d1eec49d91\scratchpad\superset-companion-design.html — ask it for an independent architectural verdict on whether this design is sound, what it would change, and its single strongest objection. Context: personal single-user Android phone + Wear OS app that mirrors AI-agent status from a Windows desktop running a fork of Superset, and lets the user answer an agent's pending question from their watch by having a desktop bridge inject keystrokes into the agent's terminal. Public Cloudflare Tunnel transport, FCM push, per-request HMAC + AES-GCM sealed bodies, QR pairing. Save the response to tmp/llm-responses/.

content.text: Reading DESIGN.html fully.

content.content:
1 2 3 4 5 6 superset-companion — Design 7 8 9 57 58
59 60

superset-companion

61

A personal Android phone and Wear OS app that carries agent status off the desktop — so an agent waiting on you doesn't wait for hours.

62 63

Designv1 64 Repo C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion · Desktop fork-superset-windows-arm64 · 28 July 2026

65 66

The problem

67 68

Agents run in Superset terminals all day. When one needs input it turns red and stops — sometimes for hours, because you're not at the machine. The desktop already computes exactly the signal that matters; it just has no way to reach you.

69 70

The watch does one job: buzz when an agent is blocked, show the whole question, take your answer. The phone does the fuller job: the agent tree, readable chats, and a reply box.

71 72

Scope

73 74
75 76 77 78 79 80 81 82 83 84
In v1Not in v1
Agent tree, sorted by statusCreating chats, terminals, or workspaces
Read chat transcripts on the phoneMirroring snooze / archive / pin / drag order
Send a message to an existing agentAnswering subagent questions (impossible — see below)
Answer a question from phone or watchAnswering Codex questions
Push notification on redOffline queueing of anything
85
86 87

What we proved before designing

88 89

Six assumptions were tested against the live system rather than reasoned about. Four held, two did not, and the two failures reshaped the design.

90 91
92 93 94 95 96 97 98 99 100 101 102 103
ClaimResultConsequence
host.db readable while Superset holds itProvenMust open mode=ro. immutable=1 froze at a stale value for a full 45-second poll — it would have shipped a phone that silently never updates.
/events WebSocket streams live statusProven91 messages in 60s, one global socket covers every workspace. But events arrive 2–3× duplicated and there's no snapshot on connect.
Question text and options live in the transcriptProvenMain-agent questions only. Pending vs answered is derivable exactly.
Answer bytes can drive the pickerProvenEstablished empirically by driving the real CLI in a pty. Contract below.
terminal.snapshot worksDisproven404 on the running app — it shipped in v1.18.0, released 27 July; the machine still runs 1.17.0.
.askq markers mean a question is pendingDisproven17 stale markers, oldest 21 days. Presence proves nothing; absence is still a sound veto.
Question text must be parsed out of transcriptsDisprovenThe hook already receives all of it. See below — this removed a whole subsystem.
104
105 106

The question arrives for free

107 108

Most of this design was built around reconstructing questions from transcript files — globbing ~/.claude/projects/, finding the right session, parsing JSONL. That turned out to be unnecessary. Claude Code's PreToolUse hook already hands the fork everything, at the moment the question is raised, and the fork's notify script reads the tool's name and throws the rest away.

109 110

Confirmed by capturing a real payload rather than trusting the docs:

111 112 
tool_name        AskUserQuestion
113	tool_use_id      toolu_01Jo29vFXrkYHkP8rF7EoZMK
114	transcript_path  <exact path — no globbing needed>
115	session_id, cwd, permission_mode, effort
116	agent_id         present only when a subagent asked
117	agent_type       present only when a subagent asked
118	
119	tool_input.questions[] → { question, header, multiSelect,
120	                           options[] → { label, description } }
121 122
Three things this removes. No transcript parsing for question content — it arrives structurally and instantly. No deriving the question's identity, because tool_use_id comes from the same event that created it, which is exactly what the freshness guard needs. And subagent questions stop being invisible: hooks fire inside subagents and carry agent_id, so the "we can tell you a teammate is blocked but never what it asked" limitation is simply gone.
123 124

The transcript stays in the picture as a cross-check — a hook can die mid-flight, and this machine has form for that with its ARM64 shell crashes — but it is no longer how questions are discovered.

125 126

What this does not solve is answering. A PreToolUse hook can allow, deny, rewrite the arguments or inject context; it cannot fabricate a result. Denying blocks the question and tells the agent why, which is not the same as answering it. So the keystroke path and its race remain exactly as described below.

127 128

Does the premise hold? Measured.

129 130

The design rests on an assumption worth testing before building anything: that a useful share of the questions blocking your agents are ones the phone can actually answer. Subagent questions can't be — their text never touches disk. If most of your questions came from teammates, the watch would be a buzzer that says "go to your desk", and the whole thing would be worth much less.

131 132

So it was measured against your last seven days rather than estimated.

133 134
135 136 137 138 139 140 141 142 143 144 145
MeasurementResultMeaning
Questions that blocked an agent300 across 44 sessionsRoughly 30–80 a day
Answerable from disk293 of 300 — 97.7%The phone is an answerer, not a buzzer
Organic subagent questionsZeroAll 7 unanswerable came from this design session's own probe agents
Question lengthmedian 1,412 chars; 64% over 1,024The native watch app is justified by data, not assumption
Several questions in one prompt59%The majority case — must be supported early
Multi-select~10%Genuinely a tail case
146
147 148
Both load-bearing assumptions survived contact with the data. Nearly everything that blocks you is answerable remotely, and nearly two-thirds of questions would be silently truncated by a bridged notification — which is exactly the failure the native watch app exists to prevent.
149 150

Notification volume — the thing that would kill it

151 152

Thirty to eighty questions a day, and most of them you answer at the desk within seconds. Pushing every red would mean roughly fifty buzzes a day for questions you were already handling, and a watch that buzzes fifty times a day gets muted within a week. Muted is the same as not built.

153 154

So a red doesn't push immediately. It pushes only if it's still unanswered after three minutes — long enough that anything you deal with at the desk never reaches your wrist, short enough that a genuinely blocked agent still finds you before it has been sitting idle for long. The notification you get then means something specific: nobody has dealt with this.

155 156

A second push retracts it when a question is answered anywhere, so a notification never outlives the thing it was about. A sweep on app foreground alone wouldn't do — the likeliest stale buzz comes from a phone that was dozing.

157 158

Architecture

159 160 
Pixel Watch 4        Pixel 10 Pro Fold        Cloudflare       mk-xps (Windows)
161	┌────────────┐       ┌─────────────────┐      ┌─────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
162	│ question   │◄─────►│ phone app       │◄────►│  edge   │◄────►│ companion bridge │
163	│ screen     │ Data  │ Kotlin/Compose  │ HTTPS│ +Access │tunnel│  in host-service │
164	└────────────┘ Layer │ cache           │  WSS └─────────┘      └────────┬─────────┘
165	                     └────────▲────────┘                       same process, so
166	                              │                                verify+write can
167	                        FCM ──┘  opaque event id only          hold one lock
168
169 170
    171
  • FCM wakes the phone on red. The only push pipe on stock Android that survives Doze without your app holding a socket, and free. Payload is ~120 bytes of opaque ids — no question text ever reaches Google.
    • 172
  • Cloudflare Tunnel carries everything interactive. cloudflared dials outbound, so there are no inbound ports and no origin IP to attack.
    • 173
  • Data Layer carries phone ↔ watch. The watch has no independent path to the desktop, so it works wherever your phone works — including away from home, but not without the phone.
    • 174
175 176

Where the bridge lives

177 178

Inside host-service, as a fork-owned module with its own fixed loopback listener. The port is fixed and fails loud if taken — cloudflared's ingress rule is static, so silently picking another port would leave the tunnel pointing at nothing, presenting as "phone says offline" with no explanation.

179 180
This placement is what makes safe answering possible at all. The alternative — a bridge in the Electron main process — would have to verify the screen and then write via two separate calls into host-service, with no lock between them. Every guard would prove the picker was there at the moment of checking, not at the moment of writing, and that gap is exactly where the stale-answer failures live. Sharing a process means verification and the keystroke can happen as one operation under a per-terminal lock, so a keystroke arriving from the desktop at the same instant serialises behind it instead of racing it.

181

The cost is merge burden: host-service is upstream-owned, so the module needs its logic in fork-only files with the smallest possible mount surface, each behind a FEATURES.md marker, and calls into upstream internals funnelled through one adapter so a rename breaks in one visible place.

182 183
The known hole: the bridge dies with the app. host-service watches the desktop app's PID and exits with it, while the pty daemon is detached and survives. So if Superset closes or crashes, your agents keep running and keep going red — with the bridge and FCM sender dead. You chose to accept this rather than restructure, mitigated by a phone-side liveness watchdog: if the last sync showed working agents and no heartbeat arrives for several minutes, the phone raises a local notification saying contact was lost. That converts a silent failure into something you can act on.
184 185

Status

186 187

Only coarse status is readable without the desktop app running. The rich dot state — the latched axes — and all of snooze/archive/pin/tiering live in the renderer's browser storage, unreachable from outside.

188 189

You cut the enrichment layer from v1. The phone shows the agent tree sorted by status, red first. No snooze mirroring, no pin, no drag order. That removes a renderer exporter, multi-window election, a debounce protocol, and a freshness contract — the single largest complexity item in the design — for something with no effect on the red path.

190 191
192 193 194 195 196 197 198 199
DotFromNotifies
Needs inputBase layer, always availableYes
WorkingBase layerNo
NeutralBase layer — idleNo
200
201 202

Green is deliberately absent. "Ready for review" is a review-axis concept that only exists in the renderer, and synthesising it from coarse data would be a lie. Red and yellow are honest without it.

203 204

Answering a question

205 206

This is the sharpest part of the design, and the reason so much of it looks paranoid.

207 208

The proven contract

209 210

Established by driving the real Claude Code CLI (2.1.220) in a pty across four scripted runs — not inferred from source:

211 212
    213
  • Single select: one bare digit both selects and submits. No Enter. There is no confirmation step.
    • 214
  • Several questions in one call: N digits, then Enter on the review screen.
    • 215
  • Multi-select inverts the rules: digits and space toggle; Enter toggles rather than submits; submitting is right-arrow to the Submit tab, then Enter. A naive implementation that appends Enter to "submit" silently flips a selection instead.
    • 216
  • Free text: digit N+1 opens an inline editor, then UTF-8, then Enter.
    • 217
  • Bracketed paste is inert. A wrapped digit produces cursor noise and no state change, so terminal.send cannot drive the picker at all — only raw terminal.writeInput works.
    • 218
219 220
The stale-answer hazard, reproduced three ways. When the picker is gone, stray digits land in the composer and a following Enter submits them as a real message — observed: a stray 23 became a genuine prompt the model burned a turn answering. Mid-turn, typed input is queued to steer the running agent. And with a different picker open, a digit commits instantly against the wrong question. Because digits commit atomically there is no safe retry and nothing to intercept.
221 222

The guard stack

223 224

The phone never constructs keystrokes. It sends semantic intent — a question id, a fingerprint, and chosen option indices — and the bridge owns the byte encoding, so the client is structurally incapable of emitting a stray digit. Before writing anything, the bridge checks six things:

225 226
    227
  1. The question's tool_use_id still has no tool_result in the transcript.
    2. 228
  2. The agent-session binding still matches — a /resume or restart invalidates it.
    3. 229
  3. The terminal session is still active.
    4. 230
  4. The permission axis is still latched.
    5. 231
  5. A snapshot confirms the picker is still on screen showing that question.
    6. 232
  6. The .askq marker still exists — worthless as proof, but its absence is a sound veto.
    7. 233
234 235

Any failure writes nothing and reports the question as stale. Multi-select re-verifies the screen between each keystroke, since each one can land on a changed screen. On timeout the bridge reports "unconfirmed" and never retries — a blind retry could answer a different question that has since opened, which with atomic digits is unrecoverable.

236 237
The guards are only sound if they're a transaction, not a checklist. Checking six conditions and then writing is two separate acts; everything can pass and the screen can still change before the byte lands. So the whole sequence — read the screen, evaluate the guards, write — runs inside host-service holding a lock. This is why the bridge lives there and not in the Electron main process.
238 239
The lock covers the whole answer, not each keystroke. Locking per keystroke is not enough, and the failure is worth stating because it is counter-intuitive: in a multi-select question, digits toggle. If your phone answers {1,2} while your watch answers {1,3}, perfectly serialised keystrokes interleave into {2,3} — an answer neither device chose, with every guard passing before every byte. So one answer holds one lease for its entire sequence, and a second device attempting the same question is refused outright rather than queued.
240 241
What remains, stated honestly. A keystroke injector cannot prove which screen will consume the next byte. If you press Escape at the desktop microseconds before the bridge takes its lease, that keystroke is already sitting in the pty daemon's queue while the bridge's screen mirror hasn't seen the repaint — every guard passes, then Escape closes the question, then the digit lands somewhere else. The mirror is downstream of the very queue being raced, so no lock inside the bridge can order them. You've accepted this: it's a personal machine, the window is small, and the mitigation is that every injected write is logged with the guard state that permitted it, so any incident is reconstructable rather than mysterious.
242 243
Two guards rest on an unauthenticated endpoint. The agent-binding check and the permission-state check both read a store written by notifications.hook, which is deliberately unauthenticated on localhost, and every agent shell has its URL in the environment. So an agent that reads untrusted content and follows instructions in it could forge a "question is pending" state for any terminal. This grants no privilege a local process doesn't already have, but it means those two guards must never be the load-bearing ones — the transcript check and the screen check are, and both are outside that endpoint's reach.
244 245
Interaction is online-only. Nothing queues — not answers, not messages. An answer is a time-sensitive keystroke whose meaning depends on the live screen, so executing it minutes later against a different screen is the wrong contract regardless of how it's guarded. Offline, the app shows the cached tree and refuses to send. You refetch and tap again.
246 247

What can't be answered

248 249

Codex terminals are out of scope for answering in v1 — the byte contract was established against Claude Code and none of it generalises. They still appear in the tree with status, and still notify.

250 251

Everything else is answerable, subagent questions included, now that the hook payload turns out to carry their text and their identity.

252 253

What a shipping product did instead

254 255

ADE is an open-source macOS workspace solving almost exactly this problem — agents in worktrees, an iPhone companion, approving work from your phone. Over a thousand commits and several releases a day, so its choices carry weight.

256 257

It runs Claude through the Agent SDK, gets structured questions for free, and renders real buttons on the phone. Where an agent runs in a terminal instead, it ships a full terminal emulator with keystroke passthrough and lets a human drive it — and it explicitly refuses to answer a terminal prompt on the user's behalf, with code that throws rather than guess, because "ADE cannot answer them truthfully".

258 259
Why we're doing the thing they refused. ADE owns its agents from birth, so it never has to attach to one already running. This fork's entire value — the dots, worktrees, auto-resume, Codex support, the terminal panes themselves — is built on agents that are already running when we arrive. The structured route isn't available to us, for the same reason the repo's own ACP path isn't. Their refusal is right for their architecture, and it's a fair warning about ours.
260 261

Several of their patterns are worth taking directly, and are folded into the design above: never retry an ambiguous send — report it unconfirmed and drop it, rather than risk typing twice; one input in flight per session with a stable id the host de-duplicates; capability negotiation that degrades to a reduced feature set rather than refusing the connection, because an auto-updating phone will meet an out-of-date desktop; a pairing QR whose payload sits in the URL fragment so it never reaches a server; and a delivery policy where ongoing work stays ambient and only genuine attention notifies, with a desktop you're sitting at suppressing the phone alert until the next heartbeat escalates it.

262 263

The alternative that was seriously considered

264 265

An independent review argued the whole keystroke approach should be abandoned in favour of the repo's ACP sessions path, which already turns a question into a structured request with an id and first-answer-wins resolution — no keystrokes, no race at all. That's a strong argument and it was investigated properly rather than dismissed.

266 267

It's real code, not vapour: the adapter package is installed on this machine, and the feature gate that disables it is a single fork-owned line. But it cannot do the job, for a reason no amount of enabling fixes.

268 269
    270
  • It can't attach to a running agent. An ACP session spawns its own agent process over stdio. There is no attach-to-terminal path anywhere in it — so a session created from your phone is a different conversation from the one currently blocking you. It doesn't answer the question you're looking at.
    • 271
  • The status dots would go dark. The notify hook self-skips without a terminal id in its environment, and ACP children never get one. Hooks fire and do nothing.
    • 272
  • There's no desktop UI for it. Searching the desktop app for any ACP reference returns nothing; the docs say so outright. Its only client is the iOS-only mobile app.
    • 273
  • It would delete most of the fork. Auto-resume, terminal links, Codex support and the entire dot subsystem are terminal-bound by construction.
    • 274
275 276
The right conclusion, and the thing worth stealing. ACP is not the wrong quality — it's the wrong tool. But its resolution semantics are exactly what this design needs, so the bridge copies them rather than reinventing: a stable request id, first-answer-wins, and an explicit "already resolved" status instead of a silent failure. That is precisely the answer-wide lease described above, and it's proven design rather than a guess.
277 278

Security

279 280

The bridge is on the public internet and terminal write is arbitrary code execution on your desktop. Every reviewer independently said a bearer token alone is not enough, and the hostname becomes public knowledge the moment the TLS certificate hits Certificate Transparency logs.

281 282

Four independent layers:

283 284
    285
  • Cloudflare Access with a service token, so scanners and brute force die at the edge and never reach your desktop. Revocable from Cloudflare independently of the phone. The bridge also validates the Access JWT rather than trusting the edge, because a policy misconfiguration can otherwise let requests through.
    • 286
  • Sealed, replay-bound requests. Bodies are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with the timestamp, nonce, method and path bound into the cipher's associated data. That gives confidentiality, integrity and replay protection from one primitive rather than layering a separate signature over the top — fewer things to get subtly wrong, and no separate canonicalisation format to mismatch. A nonce cache outliving the freshness window is what actually stops replay; the timestamp alone would not.
    • 287
  • Writes go over HTTP, never the WebSocket. Authenticating a WebSocket handshake says nothing about individual frames sent later, so the socket carries reads only and every write is its own sealed request. Writes are rare enough that this costs nothing.
    • 288
  • Pairing establishes the long-term key rather than transmitting it. The QR carries a short-lived pairing code, and the lasting key is derived through a key exchange — so the secret is never rendered on a screen where a photo, a screenshot in a cloud backup, or someone behind you captures it whole. The Cloudflare service token is bound to the device during that exchange rather than printed in the same blob.
    • 289
  • Keystore-bound storage on the phone, with the key requiring device authentication. A stolen locked phone yields nothing usable.
    • 290
291 292

Beyond the wire: writes are rate-limited far more tightly than reads (10/min versus 120/min), every injected write is appended to an audit log before it executes, the bridge refuses to write to plain shells (only terminals with an agent binding), free-text sends require a biometric confirmation while option taps don't, and there's a desktop panic switch that strips write access without unpairing.

293 294

Certificate pinning is deliberately rejected: Cloudflare's certificates last 90 days and Cloudflare controls the issuing authorities, so pinning breaks the app on a schedule — and for a sideloaded app with no update channel, that means it fails exactly when you need it.

295 296
Blast radius, stated plainly. Anyone holding the pairing key can type into your agent terminals from anywhere on earth. The layers change how reachable and how detectable that is, not the consequence. Revocation is from the desktop and takes effect on the next request.
297 298
One recommendation worth acting on separately. Your (BUILD-REPAIR) loop lets an unattended agent edit any non-frozen file, and your own notes say containment is not semantic review. This code is internet-exposed, holds credentials, and can type into terminals. The pairing, crypto, edge and injection directories should join the frozen-paths list — a genuine bug there should fail loud for you, not get silently "repaired" by an agent reading a build log an attacker may have influenced.
299 300

Client

301 302

Native Kotlin, one Gradle project, phone and watch sharing an applicationId and keystore — the Data Layer silently delivers nothing if either differs.

303 304

Phone: home (agent tree, red first), chat detail, question sheet, pairing, diagnostics. Home and chat sit in one adaptive scaffold so the Fold's inner screen shows both panes and the cover screen shows one. Selection survives folding via saved state, not remember.

305 306

Chat reads conversationally: your messages and the agent's replies, with tool calls collapsed to a one-line chip you can tap to expand.

307 308

Question sheet: header, full question, options as large buttons with their full descriptions unclamped, and the last ten messages scrollable above for context. Single-select taps submit; multi-select uses checkboxes and an explicit Submit, because training you on tap-to-submit and then showing checkboxes would fire three separate answers.

309 310

Watch: one question screen, uncapped and scrollable. This is why it's a real app rather than a bridged notification — Android clamps notification strings to 1024 characters and truncates silently, so you'd answer a question whose second half you never saw.

311 312

Every answer shows three states — pending, confirmed, or failed — never collapsed into "sent". Notifications retract when a question is answered anywhere, including a full sweep every time the app foregrounds, since the likeliest stale notification comes from a push missed while dozing.

313 314

Prerequisites

315 316
317

1. Create a Firebase project. Free Spark plan, no card. Only you can create it; the service-account credential then lives on the desktop only.

318

2. Install cloudflared. Not currently on the machine. Create a named tunnel and a DNS record on khaira.family, which is already on Cloudflare. Run it as a Windows service.

319

3. Configure Cloudflare Access with a service-token policy on the bridge hostname.

320
321 322

Installing v1.18.0 is not a prerequisite. The bridge ships inside the desktop app, so whatever release carries the bridge carries terminal.snapshot too. It only matters if you want to test against the running app before then.

323 324

Build order

325 326

Each step is demonstrable on its own, and the first three carry no write risk at all — which is the right place to stop if the byte contract needs more soak time.

327 328
    329
  1. Keep-awake first. The Windows power request that holds the desktop open while agents work. It doesn't exist yet, and without it the liveness watchdog fires on every ordinary sleep — several false alarms a day, muted within a week, and then useless when it matters.
    2. 330
  2. Bridge, tunnel, pairing, crypto, read-only API. No write path exists yet.
    3. 331
  3. Phone UI on fake data — tree, question sheet, every connection state. Needs no bridge, so it runs in parallel.
    4. 332
  4. Real reads plus delayed push. Pairing by QR, live tree, live transcripts, and notifications that only fire for questions still unanswered after the delay.
    5. 333
  5. Answer injection behind the leased verify-and-write, covering single-select and several-questions-in-one-prompt — that second case is 59% of your questions, so leaving it out would make the majority unanswerable.
    6. 334
  6. Watch app — question screen, answer path, bridged-notification suppression.
    7. 335
  7. Multi-select and free text last, each holding an answer-wide lease. Roughly 10% of questions; until then they say "answer at the desk".
    8. 336
337 338

Open risks

339 340
    341
  • The byte contract is a private contract with a TUI. Claude Code auto-updates, and a release could change picker input, wrapping or focus behaviour silently. It needs a canary test per upgrade — particularly the multi-select inversion, which is invisible in code review.
    • 342
  • Desktop sleep kills the tunnel, which is why keep-awake is the first build step rather than a later polish item. Without it the liveness watchdog cries wolf several times a day and gets muted.
    • 343
  • Long questions may not fit the visible screen. The snapshot reads what the terminal is currently showing; a question longer than the window was never retained in scrollback. Structured transcript data is the primary source for question text for exactly this reason, with the screen used for verification.
    • 344
  • Wear notification bridging on a real Pixel Watch 4 is the most likely thing to be wrong, and needs live-device verification — including what happens between installing the watch app and first launching it.
    • 345
  • The public endpoint will be scanned continuously. The app must distinguish "blocked at Cloudflare" from "desktop offline", or you'll go poke a machine that was fine.
    • 346
  • Most early time will go somewhere unglamorous — Windows sleep and resume, cloudflared startup ordering, token rotation, clock skew, and re-pairing. Budget for it.
    • 347
  • Freeze the sensitive paths from BUILD-REPAIR before the first nightly that contains them. This code is internet-exposed, holds credentials, and can type into terminals; an unattended repair agent reading a build log should not be able to edit it.
    • 348
349 350

Where this landed

351 352

Six assumptions were tested against the live system and two failed. Three independent reviewers attacked the design, and between them they found a race that survives locking, two guards resting on a forgeable endpoint, a notification volume problem that would have killed the product quietly, and a simpler architecture worth taking seriously enough to investigate properly before rejecting.

353 354

The premise itself was measured rather than assumed, and it held: 97.7% of what blocks you is answerable, and 64% of it would be truncated by the notification path a simpler design would have used.

355 356

What remains is honest. A keystroke injector cannot prove which screen consumes the next byte, and you've accepted that residual on a personal machine with logging to make any incident reconstructable. Everything else in the design exists to make that window as small as it can be.

357 358
359 360 361

superset-companion

A personal Android phone and Wear OS app that carries agent status off the desktop — so an agent waiting on you doesn't wait for hours.

Designv1 Repo C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion · Desktop fork-superset-windows-arm64 · 28 July 2026

The problem

Agents run in Superset terminals all day. When one needs input it turns red and stops — sometimes for hours, because you're not at the machine. The desktop already computes exactly the signal that matters; it just has no way to reach you.

The watch does one job: buzz when an agent is blocked, show the whole question, take your answer. The phone does the fuller job: the agent tree, readable chats, and a reply box.

Scope

In v1Not in v1
Agent tree, sorted by statusCreating chats, terminals, or workspaces
Read chat transcripts on the phoneMirroring snooze / archive / pin / drag order
Send a message to an existing agentAnswering subagent questions (impossible — see below)
Answer a question from phone or watchAnswering Codex questions
Push notification on redOffline queueing of anything

What we proved before designing

Six assumptions were tested against the live system rather than reasoned about. Four held, two did not, and the two failures reshaped the design.

ClaimResultConsequence
host.db readable while Superset holds itProvenMust open mode=ro. immutable=1 froze at a stale value for a full 45-second poll — it would have shipped a phone that silently never updates.
/events WebSocket streams live statusProven91 messages in 60s, one global socket covers every workspace. But events arrive 2–3× duplicated and there's no snapshot on connect.
Question text and options live in the transcriptProvenMain-agent questions only. Pending vs answered is derivable exactly.
Answer bytes can drive the pickerProvenEstablished empirically by driving the real CLI in a pty. Contract below.
terminal.snapshot worksDisproven404 on the running app — it shipped in v1.18.0, released 27 July; the machine still runs 1.17.0.
.askq markers mean a question is pendingDisproven17 stale markers, oldest 21 days. Presence proves nothing; absence is still a sound veto.
Question text must be parsed out of transcriptsDisprovenThe hook already receives all of it. See below — this removed a whole subsystem.

The question arrives for free

Most of this design was built around reconstructing questions from transcript files — globbing ~/.claude/projects/, finding the right session, parsing JSONL. That turned out to be unnecessary. Claude Code's PreToolUse hook already hands the fork everything, at the moment the question is raised, and the fork's notify script reads the tool's name and throws the rest away.

Confirmed by capturing a real payload rather than trusting the docs:

tool_name        AskUserQuestion
tool_use_id      toolu_01Jo29vFXrkYHkP8rF7EoZMK
transcript_path  <exact path — no globbing needed>
session_id, cwd, permission_mode, effort
agent_id         present only when a subagent asked
agent_type       present only when a subagent asked

tool_input.questions[] → { question, header, multiSelect,
                           options[] → { label, description } }
Three things this removes. No transcript parsing for question content — it arrives structurally and instantly. No deriving the question's identity, because tool_use_id comes from the same event that created it, which is exactly what the freshness guard needs. And subagent questions stop being invisible: hooks fire inside subagents and carry agent_id, so the "we can tell you a teammate is blocked but never what it asked" limitation is simply gone.

The transcript stays in the picture as a cross-check — a hook can die mid-flight, and this machine has form for that with its ARM64 shell crashes — but it is no longer how questions are discovered.

What this does not solve is answering. A PreToolUse hook can allow, deny, rewrite the arguments or inject context; it cannot fabricate a result. Denying blocks the question and tells the agent why, which is not the same as answering it. So the keystroke path and its race remain exactly as described below.

Does the premise hold? Measured.

The design rests on an assumption worth testing before building anything: that a useful share of the questions blocking your agents are ones the phone can actually answer. Subagent questions can't be — their text never touches disk. If most of your questions came from teammates, the watch would be a buzzer that says "go to your desk", and the whole thing would be worth much less.

So it was measured against your last seven days rather than estimated.

MeasurementResultMeaning
Questions that blocked an agent300 across 44 sessionsRoughly 30–80 a day
Answerable from disk293 of 300 — 97.7%The phone is an answerer, not a buzzer
Organic subagent questionsZeroAll 7 unanswerable came from this design session's own probe agents
Question lengthmedian 1,412 chars; 64% over 1,024The native watch app is justified by data, not assumption
Several questions in one prompt59%The majority case — must be supported early
Multi-select~10%Genuinely a tail case
Both load-bearing assumptions survived contact with the data. Nearly everything that blocks you is answerable remotely, and nearly two-thirds of questions would be silently truncated by a bridged notification — which is exactly the failure the native watch app exists to prevent.

Notification volume — the thing that would kill it

Thirty to eighty questions a day, and most of them you answer at the desk within seconds. Pushing every red would mean roughly fifty buzzes a day for questions you were already handling, and a watch that buzzes fifty times a day gets muted within a week. Muted is the same as not built.

So a red doesn't push immediately. It pushes only if it's still unanswered after three minutes — long enough that anything you deal with at the desk never reaches your wrist, short enough that a genuinely blocked agent still finds you before it has been sitting idle for long. The notification you get then means something specific: nobody has dealt with this.

A second push retracts it when a question is answered anywhere, so a notification never outlives the thing it was about. A sweep on app foreground alone wouldn't do — the likeliest stale buzz comes from a phone that was dozing.

Architecture

Pixel Watch 4        Pixel 10 Pro Fold        Cloudflare       mk-xps (Windows)
┌────────────┐       ┌─────────────────┐      ┌─────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│ question   │◄─────►│ phone app       │◄────►│  edge   │◄────►│ companion bridge │
│ screen     │ Data  │ Kotlin/Compose  │ HTTPS│ +Access │tunnel│  in host-service │
└────────────┘ Layer │ cache           │  WSS └─────────┘      └────────┬─────────┘
                     └────────▲────────┘                       same process, so
                              │                                verify+write can
                        FCM ──┘  opaque event id only          hold one lock
  • FCM wakes the phone on red. The only push pipe on stock Android that survives Doze without your app holding a socket, and free. Payload is ~120 bytes of opaque ids — no question text ever reaches Google.
  • Cloudflare Tunnel carries everything interactive. cloudflared dials outbound, so there are no inbound ports and no origin IP to attack.
  • Data Layer carries phone ↔ watch. The watch has no independent path to the desktop, so it works wherever your phone works — including away from home, but not without the phone.

Where the bridge lives

Inside host-service, as a fork-owned module with its own fixed loopback listener. The port is fixed and fails loud if taken — cloudflared's ingress rule is static, so silently picking another port would leave the tunnel pointing at nothing, presenting as "phone says offline" with no explanation.

This placement is what makes safe answering possible at all. The alternative — a bridge in the Electron main process — would have to verify the screen and then write via two separate calls into host-service, with no lock between them. Every guard would prove the picker was there at the moment of checking, not at the moment of writing, and that gap is exactly where the stale-answer failures live. Sharing a process means verification and the keystroke can happen as one operation under a per-terminal lock, so a keystroke arriving from the desktop at the same instant serialises behind it instead of racing it.

The cost is merge burden: host-service is upstream-owned, so the module needs its logic in fork-only files with the smallest possible mount surface, each behind a FEATURES.md marker, and calls into upstream internals funnelled through one adapter so a rename breaks in one visible place.

The known hole: the bridge dies with the app. host-service watches the desktop app's PID and exits with it, while the pty daemon is detached and survives. So if Superset closes or crashes, your agents keep running and keep going red — with the bridge and FCM sender dead. You chose to accept this rather than restructure, mitigated by a phone-side liveness watchdog: if the last sync showed working agents and no heartbeat arrives for several minutes, the phone raises a local notification saying contact was lost. That converts a silent failure into something you can act on.

Status

Only coarse status is readable without the desktop app running. The rich dot state — the latched axes — and all of snooze/archive/pin/tiering live in the renderer's browser storage, unreachable from outside.

You cut the enrichment layer from v1. The phone shows the agent tree sorted by status, red first. No snooze mirroring, no pin, no drag order. That removes a renderer exporter, multi-window election, a debounce protocol, and a freshness contract — the single largest complexity item in the design — for something with no effect on the red path.

DotFromNotifies
Needs inputBase layer, always availableYes
WorkingBase layerNo
NeutralBase layer — idleNo

Green is deliberately absent. "Ready for review" is a review-axis concept that only exists in the renderer, and synthesising it from coarse data would be a lie. Red and yellow are honest without it.

So the whole sequence — read the screen, evaluate the guards, write — runs inside host-service holding a lock. This is why the bridge lives there and not in the Electron main process.

Offline, the app shows the cached tree and refuses to send. You refetch and tap again.

What can't be answered

Codex terminals are out of scope for answering in v1 — the byte contract was established against Claude Code and none of it generalises. They still appear in the tree with status, and still notify.

Everything else is answerable, subagent questions included, now that the hook payload turns out to carry their text and their identity.

What a shipping product did instead

ADE is an open-source macOS workspace solving almost exactly this problem — agents in worktrees, an iPhone companion, approving work from your phone. Over a thousand commits and several releases a day, so its choices carry weight.

It runs Claude through the Agent SDK, gets structured questions for free, and renders real buttons on the phone. Where an agent runs in a terminal instead, it ships a full terminal emulator with keystroke passthrough and lets a human drive it — and it explicitly refuses to answer a terminal prompt on the user's behalf, with code that throws rather than guess, because "ADE cannot answer them truthfully".

Why we're doing the thing they refused. ADE owns its agents from birth, so it never has to attach to one already running. This fork's entire value — the dots, worktrees, auto-resume, Codex support, the terminal panes themselves — is built on agents that are already running when we arrive. The structured route isn't available to us, for the same reason the repo's own ACP path isn't. Their refusal is right for their architecture, and it's a fair warning about ours.

Several of their patterns are worth taking directly, and are folded into the design above: never retry an ambiguous send — report it unconfirmed and drop it, rather than risk typing twice; one input in flight per session with a stable id the host de-duplicates; capability negotiation that degrades to a reduced feature set rather than refusing the connection, because an auto-updating phone will meet an out-of-date desktop; a pairing QR whose payload sits in the URL fragment so it never reaches a server; and a delivery policy where ongoing work stays ambient and only genuine attention notifies, with a desktop you're sitting at suppressing the phone alert until the next heartbeat escalates it.

The alternative that was seriously considered

An independent review argued the whole keystroke approach should be abandoned in favour of the repo's ACP sessions path, which already turns a question into a structured request with an id and first-answer-wins resolution — no keystrokes, no race at all. That's a strong argument and it was investigated properly rather than dismissed.

It's real code, not vapour: the adapter package is installed on this machine, and the feature gate that disables it is a single fork-owned line. But it cannot do the job, for a reason no amount of enabling fixes.

  • It can't attach to a running agent. An ACP session spawns its own agent process over stdio. There is no attach-to-terminal path anywhere in it — so a session created from your phone is a different conversation from the one currently blocking you. It doesn't answer the question you're looking at.
  • The status dots would go dark. The notify hook self-skips without a terminal id in its environment, and ACP children never get one. Hooks fire and do nothing.
  • There's no desktop UI for it. Searching the desktop app for any ACP reference returns nothing; the docs say so outright. Its only client is the iOS-only mobile app.
  • It would delete most of the fork. Auto-resume, terminal links, Codex support and the entire dot subsystem are terminal-bound by construction.
The right conclusion, and the thing worth stealing. ACP is not the wrong quality — it's the wrong tool. But its resolution semantics are exactly what this design needs, so the bridge copies them rather than reinventing: a stable request id, first-answer-wins, and an explicit "already resolved" status instead of a silent failure. That is precisely the answer-wide lease described above, and it's proven design rather than a guess.

Security

The bridge is on the public internet and terminal write is arbitrary code execution on your desktop. Every reviewer independently said a bearer token alone is not enough, and the hostname becomes public knowledge the moment the TLS certificate hits Certificate Transparency logs.

Four independent layers:

  • Cloudflare Access with a service token, so scanners and brute force die at the edge and never reach your desktop. Revocable from Cloudflare independently of the phone. The bridge also validates the Access JWT rather than trusting the edge, because a policy misconfiguration can otherwise let requests through.
  • Sealed, replay-bound requests. Bodies are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with the timestamp, nonce, method and path bound into the cipher's associated data. That gives confidentiality, integrity and replay protection from one primitive rather than layering a separate signature over the top — fewer things to get subtly wrong, and no separate canonicalisation format to mismatch. A nonce cache outliving the freshness window is what actually stops replay; the timestamp alone would not.
  • Writes go over HTTP, never the WebSocket. Authenticating a WebSocket handshake says nothing about individual frames sent later, so the socket carries reads only and every write is its own sealed request. Writes are rare enough that this costs nothing.
  • Pairing establishes the long-term key rather than transmitting it. The QR carries a short-lived pairing code, and the lasting key is derived through a key exchange — so the secret is never rendered on a screen where a photo, a screenshot in a cloud backup, or someone behind you captures it whole. The Cloudflare service token is bound to the device during that exchange rather than printed in the same blob.
  • Keystore-bound storage on the phone, with the key requiring device authentication. A stolen locked phone yields nothing usable.

Beyond the wire: writes are rate-limited far more tightly than reads (10/min versus 120/min), every injected write is appended to an audit log before it executes, the bridge refuses to write to plain shells (only terminals with an agent binding), free-text sends require a biometric confirmation while option taps don't, and there's a desktop panic switch that strips write access without unpairing.

Certificate pinning is deliberately rejected: Cloudflare's certificates last 90 days and Cloudflare controls the issuing authorities, so pinning breaks the app on a schedule — and for a sideloaded app with no update channel, that means it fails exactly when you need it.

Blast radius, stated plainly. Anyone holding the pairing key can type into your agent terminals from anywhere on earth. The layers change how reachable and how detectable that is, not the consequence. Revocation is from the desktop and takes effect on the next request.
One recommendation worth acting on separately. Your (BUILD-REPAIR) loop lets an unattended agent edit any non-frozen file, and your own notes say containment is not semantic review. This code is internet-exposed, holds credentials, and can type into terminals. The pairing, crypto, edge and injection directories should join the frozen-paths list — a genuine bug there should fail loud for you, not get silently "repaired" by an agent reading a build log an attacker may have influenced.

Client

Native Kotlin, one Gradle project, phone and watch sharing an applicationId and keystore — the Data Layer silently delivers nothing if either differs.

Phone: home (agent tree, red first), chat detail, question sheet, pairing, diagnostics. Home and chat sit in one adaptive scaffold so the Fold's inner screen shows both panes and the cover screen shows one. Selection survives folding via saved state, not remember.

Chat reads conversationally: your messages and the agent's replies, with tool calls collapsed to a one-line chip you can tap to expand.

Question sheet: header, full question, options as large buttons with their full descriptions unclamped, and the last ten messages scrollable above for context. Single-select taps submit; multi-select uses checkboxes and an explicit Submit, because training you on tap-to-submit and then showing checkboxes would fire three separate answers.

Watch: one question screen, uncapped and scrollable. This is why it's a real app rather than a bridged notification — Android clamps notification strings to 1024 characters and truncates silently, so you'd answer a question whose second half you never saw.

Every answer shows three states — pending, confirmed, or failed — never collapsed into "sent". Notifications retract when a question is answered anywhere, including a full sweep every time the app foregrounds, since the likeliest stale notification comes from a push missed while dozing.

Prerequisites

1. Create a Firebase project. Free Spark plan, no card. Only you can create it; the service-account credential then lives on the desktop only.

2. Install cloudflared. Not currently on the machine. Create a named tunnel and a DNS record on khaira.family, which is already on Cloudflare. Run it as a Windows service.

3. Configure Cloudflare Access with a service-token policy on the bridge hostname.

Installing v1.18.0 is not a prerequisite. The bridge ships inside the desktop app, so whatever release carries the bridge carries terminal.snapshot too. It only matters if you want to test against the running app before then.

Build order

Each step is demonstrable on its own, and the first three carry no write risk at all — which is the right place to stop if the byte contract needs more soak time.

  1. Keep-awake first. The Windows power request that holds the desktop open while agents work. It doesn't exist yet, and without it the liveness watchdog fires on every ordinary sleep — several false alarms a day, muted within a week, and then useless when it matters.
  2. Bridge, tunnel, pairing, crypto, read-only API. No write path exists yet.
  3. Phone UI on fake data — tree, question sheet, every connection state. Needs no bridge, so it runs in parallel.
  4. Real reads plus delayed push. Pairing by QR, live tree, live transcripts, and notifications that only fire for questions still unanswered after the delay.
  5. Answer injection behind the leased verify-and-write, covering single-select and several-questions-in-one-prompt — that second case is 59% of your questions, so leaving it out would make the majority unanswerable.
  6. Watch app — question screen, answer path, bridged-notification suppression.
  7. Multi-select and free text last, each holding an answer-wide lease. Roughly 10% of questions; until then they say "answer at the desk".

Open risks

  • The byte contract is a private contract with a TUI. Claude Code auto-updates, and a release could change picker input, wrapping or focus behaviour silently. It needs a canary test per upgrade — particularly the multi-select inversion, which is invisible in code review.
  • Desktop sleep kills the tunnel, which is why keep-awake is the first build step rather than a later polish item. Without it the liveness watchdog cries wolf several times a day and gets muted.
  • Long questions may not fit the visible screen. The snapshot reads what the terminal is currently showing; a question longer than the window was never retained in scrollback. Structured transcript data is the primary source for question text for exactly this reason, with the screen used for verification.
  • Wear notification bridging on a real Pixel Watch 4 is the most likely thing to be wrong, and needs live-device verification — including what happens between installing the watch app and first launching it.
  • The public endpoint will be scanned continuously. The app must distinguish "blocked at Cloudflare" from "desktop offline", or you'll go poke a machine that was fine.
  • Most early time will go somewhere unglamorous — Windows sleep and resume, cloudflared startup ordering, token rotation, clock skew, and re-pairing. Budget for it.
  • Freeze the sensitive paths from BUILD-REPAIR before the first nightly that contains them. This code is internet-exposed, holds credentials, and can type into terminals; an unattended repair agent reading a build log should not be able to edit it.

Where this landed

Six assumptions were tested against the live system and two failed. Three independent reviewers attacked the design, and between them they found a race that survives locking, two guards resting on a forgeable endpoint, a notification volume problem that would have killed the product quietly, and a simpler architecture worth taking seriously enough to investigate properly before rejecting.

The premise itself was measured rather than assumed, and it held: 97.7% of what blocks you is answerable, and 64% of it would be truncated by the notification path a simpler design would have used.

What remains is honest. A keystroke injector cannot prove which screen consumes the next byte, and you've accepted that residual on a personal machine with logging to make any incident reconstructable. Everything else in the design exists to make that window as small as it can be.

input.name: cf-access-setup
input.prompt:
Configure Cloudflare Access for the superset-companion bridge by driving the user's Chrome through the chrome-control bridge. The user is already logged into the Cloudflare dashboard in their Chrome (or a saved session exists). Work autonomously; only stop if you hit a login wall or CAPTCHA you cannot pass — then report exactly what you see.

## Goal (two objects in Cloudflare Zero Trust)

1. A **service token** named `superset-companion-phone`.
2. A **self-hosted Access application** protecting hostname `superset.khaira.family` (zone `khaira.family`, already on Cloudflare) with a single **Service Auth** policy that allows ONLY that service token. No allow-all rules, no identity policies.

Also capture the **application AUD tag** and the **team domain** (e.g. `<team>.cloudflareaccess.com`) — the desktop bridge will validate the Access JWT itself and needs both.

## Tooling — chrome-control bridge (already running)

A CDP bridge is already listening on port 17400 (started earlier this session; Chrome control prompt already approved). Use the CLI:

```
uv run "C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/mk-skills/chrome-control/scripts/chrome_control_bridge.py" <subcommand> --bridge-port 17400 ...
```

Steps:
1. `start --bridge-port 17400` (idempotent — expect `already_running: true`), then `check --bridge-port 17400`. If the bridge is NOT running, start will launch it; if Chrome shows a control prompt the user must approve, report and stop.
2. `attach --bridge-port 17400 --url "https://one.dash.cloudflare.com/"` — capture the returned sessionId. If an existing Zero Trust tab exists you may instead use `attach --reuse-existing --match-url-substring "one.dash.cloudflare.com"`.
3. Drive the page with `eval` (`--session-id <sid> --expression "<js>"`) and clicks. IMPORTANT caveats:
   - Set `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` in the environment for every call (dashboard text contains non-ASCII that crashes cp1252). In bash: `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 uv run ...`.
   - `click` uses JS element.click() which lacks user activation. Cloudflare dashboard buttons are normal SPA buttons so it usually works, but if a click "does nothing", fall back to raw CDP mouse events: eval to get the element's getBoundingClientRect center, then two `cdp --method Input.dispatchMouseEvent` calls (`mousePressed` then `mouseReleased`, button left, clickCount 1, at that x/y). Scroll element into view first if off-screen.
   - After each navigation/click, poll readiness with eval (e.g. check document.readyState and presence of expected text) — SPA loads are slow; retry reads for up to ~15s before concluding an element is missing.
   - To read the page, prefer eval expressions that return compact JSON strings (querySelectorAll + map to {text, tag, testid}), stripping non-ASCII: `.replace(/[^\x20-\x7E\n]/g,'?')`.

## Navigation guidance (UI may have drifted — adapt by reading the page, do not give up because a menu label changed)

- Zero Trust dashboard: `https://one.dash.cloudflare.com/`. If it asks to pick an account, pick the one containing zone `khaira.family`.
- Service tokens live under Access → "Service auth" → "Service tokens" (recent UIs: "Access" or "Access controls" section in the left nav; sometimes under Settings). Create token: name `superset-companion-phone`, duration: choose the LONGEST available (1 year or Non-expiring if offered — prefer Non-expiring).
- **THE CLIENT SECRET IS SHOWN EXACTLY ONCE at creation.** Before clicking away from the creation result screen, extract BOTH the Client ID (`....access`) and the Client Secret from the DOM via eval and confirm you captured non-empty values. Only then proceed.
- Applications live under Access → Applications → "Add an application" → **Self-hosted**. Configure:
  - Name: `superset-companion-bridge`
  - Domain: `superset.khaira.family` (subdomain `superset`, domain `khaira.family`), path empty.
  - Policy: create one policy, name `phone-service-token`, **Action: Service Auth**, include rule: Service Token → select `superset-companion-phone`. Remove/skip any default Allow/identity policy. Recent UIs create policies as separate reusable objects first (Access → Policies) then attach — follow whichever flow the UI presents.
  - Leave other settings default. Save.
- After saving, open the application's overview/edit page and extract the **Application Audience (AUD) Tag** (long hex string). Also read the **team domain** from Zero Trust Settings → Custom Pages / General (`<team>.cloudflareaccess.com`) or from any Access URL shown.

## Persisting results

- Write secrets to `C:\Users\khair\.superset\companion\cloudflare-access.json` (directory already exists — the FCM key lives there). JSON with keys: `client_id`, `client_secret`, `token_name`, `token_expires`, `app_aud`, `team_domain`, `hostname`, `created`. This file is a secret of the same class as the FCM key — it must NOT go anywhere inside any git repo.
- Update `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\superset-companion\SETUP.md`: in the Cloudflare section, replace the "Still needs you: Cloudflare Access" subsection with a short "Cloudflare Access — DONE" record: token name, client id (id alone is fine to record — it is not the secret), app name, AUD tag, team domain, policy = Service Auth only, and note the secret's location at `~/.superset/companion/cloudflare-access.json`. Keep the existing style of the file. Do NOT put the client secret in SETUP.md.

## Verification (do not skip)

The tunnel is NOT currently running as a service, so you cannot expect 200s. Verify the Access layer itself:
1. `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://superset.khaira.family/` WITHOUT token headers — with Access now in front, expect a Cloudflare Access denial (302 to the team login page, or 403), NOT a 502/530. (If DNS/proxy still returns 530 that means Access didn't attach or the record isn't proxied — investigate the application domain config.)
2. Same request WITH headers `CF-Access-Client-Id: <client_id>` and `CF-Access-Client-Secret: <client_secret>` — expect it to pass Access and reach the tunnel layer, i.e. **530** (tunnel not running) rather than an Access denial. 530 with headers + denial without headers = Access is correctly configured.
Record both status codes in SETUP.md's verification note.

## Reporting

Detach your CDP session when done (`detach --session-id <sid>`) but leave the bridge running. Report back: what was created (names, client id, AUD, team domain — never the secret), the two verification status codes, exactly what you changed in SETUP.md, and any UI weirdness you had to work around. If you hit a login wall, report the exact URL and visible page state and stop — do not attempt to enter credentials.

### Deliberately NOT done yet: `cloudflared service install`

The tunnel is configured but not running permanently. That is sequencing, not an oversight — starting
it earlier would have published a live hostname that answers nothing, ahead of Cloudflare Access being
configured. Access is now in place (below), so the only remaining precondition is the bridge itself:

```powershell
cloudflared service install
```

### Cloudflare Access — DONE and VERIFIED

`superset.khaira.family` now sits behind Access, reachable only by one service token.

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| Service token name | `superset-companion-phone` |
| Client id | `c6d1295b4ed520de15de3446b9ec736b.access` |
| Client secret | **not here** — `~/.superset/companion/cloudflare-access.json` |
| Token duration | Non-expiring (`forever`; nominal expiry 2126) |
| Application | `superset-companion-bridge` (self-hosted) |
| Application AUD | `40d388403c3555b6fdc75302c99c24dffa5503fa5ac2a8f7774f30ac221ccf29` |
| Team domain | `khairm.cloudflareaccess.com` |
| Policy | `phone-service-token` — **Service Auth only** (`non_identity`), include = that one token |

The application carries exactly **one** policy. There is no identity policy and no allow-all rule, so
no human login can reach the host — only a caller holding the token. The bridge still validates the
Access JWT itself against the AUD and team domain above, rather than trusting the edge, because a
policy misconfiguration could otherwise let requests through.

**Files:**
- `~/.superset/companion/cloudflare-access.json` — **the client secret**, plus ids, AUD and team
  domain. Same class as the FCM key: outside this repo, ACL-restricted to your user account only.
  Never copy it in here. The client id above is safe to record; the secret is not.

**Verified working, not assumed.** Two live requests to `https://superset.khaira.family/`:

| Request | Status | Means |
|---|---|---|
| No headers | **403** | Access refuses anonymous callers |
| `CF-Access-Client-Id` + `CF-Access-Client-Secret` | **530** | Passed Access, then hit the missing tunnel |

The 530 is the *good* result here — it is the tunnel-not-running signal from the taxonomy above,
which proves the request got past Access to the tunnel layer. Denial without the token plus 530 with
it is exactly the shape a correct configuration produces.

Set up through the Zero Trust dashboard's own authenticated API, driven from the browser session —
no manual clicking. One gotcha: `GET`s from the page work as-is, but every mutating call is blocked
by Cloudflare's WAF with a 403 challenge page unless it carries the dashboard's own
`X-Cross-Site-Security: dash` header. Blocked attempts fail at the edge and create nothing, so the
retry was safe.

## Not started

The app itself. No Gradle project, no Kotlin, nothing — planning only so far.
See the design doc for what gets built and in what order.

async function reviewRound(roundLabel, phaseFind, phaseVerify, lenses) {
  const raw = await pipeline(
    lenses,
    (l) => agent(`${REVIEW_BASE}\n\n## YOUR REVIEW LENS: ${l.key}\n\n${l.prompt}`,
      { label: `${roundLabel}:${l.key}`, phase: phaseFind, model: 'opus', effort: 'xhigh', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA }),
    (res, lens) => {
      const items = (res && res.findings) ? res.findings : []
      if (!items.length) return []
      return parallel(items.map((f) => () =>
        agent(`${CONTEXT}

You are VERIFYING a single review finding from an adversarial reviewer. Default to REFUTING it.
Read the actual code at the cited location and decide whether the defect is REAL.

A finding is NOT real if: the code already handles it elsewhere, the reviewer misread the control flow,
it depends on a state that cannot occur, it is a style preference, or it contradicts an explicit,
deliberate decision recorded in DESIGN.html (for example: no green dot, no offline queueing, no
certificate pinning, no retry on unconfirmed, the accepted pty-daemon queue race, the accepted
'bridge dies with the app' hole, Codex answering out of scope, enrichment layer cut from v1).
Deliberate accepted limitations are NOT bugs.

A finding IS real if you can walk the actual code path and show the failure.

Lens: ${lens.key}
Severity claimed: ${f.severity}
File: ${f.file}${f.line ? ':' + f.line : ''}
Title: ${f.title}
Detail: ${f.detail}
Claimed failure scenario: ${f.failure_scenario}
Proposed fix: ${f.fix}`,
          { label: `verify:${(f.file || 'unknown').split('/').pop()}`, phase: phaseVerify, model: 'opus', effort: 'high', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA })
          .then((v) => ({ ...f, lens: lens.key, verdict: v }))
      ))
    }
  )
  const all = raw.filter(Boolean).flat().filter(Boolean)
  const confirmed = all.filter((f) => f.verdict && f.verdict.real && f.verdict.corrected_severity !== 'not-a-bug')
  log(`${roundLabel}: ${all.length} raw findings -> ${confirmed.length} confirmed after adversarial verification`)
  return confirmed
}

function groupForRepair(findings) {
  const byArea = {}
  for (const f of findings) {
    const p = (f.file || '').replace(/\\/g, '/')
    let area = 'other'
    if (p.includes('/companion/')) area = 'bridge'
    else if (p.includes('apps/desktop/src/main')) area = 'desktop-main'
    else if (p.includes('app-watch')) area = 'client-watch'
    else if (p.includes('app-phone')) area = 'client-phone'
    else if (p.includes('/core/')) area = 'client-core'
    else if (p.includes('superset-companion')) area = 'client-other'
    else if (p.includes('fork-superset')) area = 'fork-other'
    if (!byArea[area]) byArea[area] = []
    byArea[area].push(f)
  }
  return Object.keys(byArea).map((k) => ({ area: k, items: byArea[k] }))
}

function repairPrompt(group, round) {
  const list = group.items.map((f, i) =>
    `${i + 1}. [${f.verdict.corrected_severity}] ${f.file}${f.line ? ':' + f.line : ''} — ${f.title}\n   ${f.detail}\n   FAILS WHEN: ${f.failure_scenario}\n   SUGGESTED FIX: ${f.fix}\n   VERIFIER SAID: ${f.verdict.reasoning}`
  ).join('\n\n')
  return `${CONTEXT}

## REPAIR ROUND ${round} — area: ${group.area}

Every finding below survived adversarial verification: a second independent reviewer tried to refute
it and could not. Fix each one properly in the actual code.

Rules:

   weaken an assertion to make a problem disappear.

   required to make those fixes correct. Other agents are repairing other areas concurrently —
   do not touch files outside your findings' area.

 - If a finding is genuinely NOT a bug, or fixing it would violate an explicit design decision, do not
   silently skip it: state clearly in your report which one and why.
 - If two findings conflict, resolve toward the design in DESIGN.html and say so.

## FINDINGS (${group.items.length})

${list}

Report per finding: FIXED (with the file and what changed), or NOT-FIXED (with the reason).
${RETURN_RULES}`
}

start a fresh shell.

installs beside cmdline-tools.

**Ready:** JDK 21.0.12 native ARM64 + Android SDK (platform 36, build-tools 36.0.0, platform-tools) at `C:\Users\khair\dev-tools\`, persisted to User env. `winget` had failed with exit 1602 — that's a silently-dismissed UAC prompt, not a real cancellation, so portable zips sidestepped it entirely.

**Running:** workflow `wf_c201c20e-4f5`, currently Phase 0 — the scaffold agent is writing `PROTOCOL.md` (the wire contract both sides code against), the fork-side stub tree, the Gradle project, and the FEATURES.md markers. It runs alone by design so the 10 parallel implementers behind it can never race on a manifest.

One thing I'll have to clean up afterwards: the workflow process started *before* the toolchain env vars were written, and a running process never picks those up — so its final Gradle check will likely report "no JDK" incorrectly. I'll run that build myself with an explicit `JAVA_HOME` once the workflow lands, before handing anything to the Codex and Fable review rounds.

I'll pick this up automatically when the workflow completes.

content.text:
Sequence after the workflow lands:

**Mine, no input needed**
1. Real Gradle build with explicit `JAVA_HOME` — workflow's verify step will falsely report "no JDK" (its process predates the env install). Fix compile errors it surfaces.
2. Commit both repos. Companion: initial commit. Fork: straight to `main` per your rule.

**Your three review rounds, in order**
3. 3× Codex `gpt-5.6-sol` `--effort ultra` via `/call-another-llm` — review **and test**. Run in background, poll under 120s.
4. 3× Fable code-review agents.
5. `/simplify` fully.
6. Fix what they surface, re-verify, re-commit.

**Then it's still not usable until:**

| Blocker | Who |
|---|---|
| Signing keystore — phone+watch MUST share one or Data Layer silently delivers nothing | me, needs your go on where it lives |
| `cloudflared service install` — deliberately deferred until the bridge exists | me |
| BUILD-REPAIR freeze for companion crypto/pairing/edge/injection paths | you — edits `ci-repair.sh`, itself frozen, so deliberate local commit |
| Fork side ships via nightly build + Release install, never hot-patched | your green light on install timing |
| Sideload to Pixel 10 Pro Fold + Watch 4, QR pair, live test | you hold the devices |

**Biggest unknown that only hardware settles:** Wear notification bridging. Design flags it as the most likely thing to be wrong, including the window between installing the watch app and first launching it. No amount of review closes that.

**Ongoing:** byte-contract canary per Claude Code upgrade — a TUI release could silently change picker input, and the multiSelect inversion is invisible in code review.

input.content:
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

$dir = 'C:\Users\khair\.superset\companion\keystore'
$jks = Join-Path $dir 'superset-companion.jks'
$props = Join-Path $dir 'signing.properties'
$keytool = 'C:\Users\khair\dev-tools\jdk-21\bin\keytool.exe'

if (Test-Path $jks) {
  Write-Output "REFUSING: keystore already exists at $jks"
  Write-Output "Overwriting it would permanently break upgrades for anything already signed with it."
  exit 1
}

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $dir | Out-Null

# base62 password — alphanumeric only, so it never needs escaping in Gradle
# properties, command lines, or CI. 32 chars ~ 190 bits.
$alphabet = 'REDACTED'
$bytes = [byte[]]::new(64)
[System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator]::Fill($bytes)
$pw = -join (0..31 | ForEach-Object { $alphabet[$bytes[$_] % 62] })

$alias = 'superset-companion'
$dname = 'CN=superset-companion, OU=personal, O=khaira.family, C=GB'

& $keytool -genkeypair -v `
  -keystore $jks `
  -alias $alias `
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 `
  -validity 10000 `
  -storetype PKCS12 `
  -storepass $pw -keypass $pw `
  -dname $dname 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { Write-Output "keytool: $_" }

if (-not (Test-Path $jks)) { throw "keytool did not produce $jks" }

# Gradle reads this. It lives OUTSIDE both repos, like the FCM and Cloudflare secrets.
$lines = @(
  '# superset-companion release signing — SECRET, never copy into a repo.',
  '# Phone and watch MUST both sign with this exact key: the Wear Data Layer',
  '# silently delivers nothing if applicationId or signature differ.',
  '# If this file or the .jks is lost, the sideloaded app can never be updated,',
  '# only uninstalled and reinstalled. Back up this whole directory.',
  "storeFile=$($jks -replace '\\', '/')",
  "storePassword=$pw",
  "keyAlias=$alias",
  "keyPassword=$pw"
)
Set-Content -Path $props -Value $lines -Encoding UTF8

# Lock down to the current user only, mirroring the FCM / Cloudflare secrets.
& icacls $dir /inheritance:r /grant:r "$($env:USERNAME):(OI)(CI)(F)" 2>&1 | Out-Null

Write-Output "== verify =="
& $keytool -list -v -keystore $jks -storepass $pw 2>&1 |
  Select-String -Pattern 'Alias name|Creation date|Signature algorithm|Subject Public Key|Valid from|Owner' |
  ForEach-Object { Write-Output "verify: $_" }

Write-Output "== SHA-256 fingerprint (needed if Firebase ever wants it) =="
& $keytool -list -keystore $jks -storepass $pw -alias $alias 2>&1 |
  Select-String -Pattern 'SHA256' | ForEach-Object { Write-Output "fp: $_" }

Write-Output "== DONE =="
Write-Output "keystore: $jks"
Write-Output "props:    $props"
Write-Output "password: NOT PRINTED — it is in signing.properties"

import json, re, sys
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from urllib.request import urlopen, Request

GOOGLE = "https://dl.google.com/dl/android/maven2"
CENTRAL = "https://repo1.maven.org/maven2"

# (label, repo, group, artifact)
ARTIFACTS = [
    ("agp",                    GOOGLE,  "com.android.tools.build", "gradle"),
    ("googleServicesPlugin",   GOOGLE,  "com.google.gms",          "google-services"),
    ("kotlin",                 CENTRAL, "org.jetbrains.kotlin",    "kotlin-gradle-plugin"),
    ("ksp",                    CENTRAL, "com.google.devtools.ksp", "symbol-processing-gradle-plugin"),
    ("kotlinxSerializationJson", CENTRAL, "org.jetbrains.kotlinx", "kotlinx-serialization-json"),
    ("kotlinxCoroutines",      CENTRAL, "org.jetbrains.kotlinx",   "kotlinx-coroutines-android"),
    ("kotlinxDatetime",        CENTRAL, "org.jetbrains.kotlinx",   "kotlinx-datetime"),
    ("okhttp",                 CENTRAL, "com.squareup.okhttp3",    "okhttp"),
    ("composeBom",             GOOGLE,  "androidx.compose",        "compose-bom"),
    ("coreKtx",                GOOGLE,  "androidx.core",           "core-ktx"),

    ("adaptiveNavigation",     GOOGLE,  "androidx.compose.material3.adaptive", "adaptive-navigation"),
    ("material3",              GOOGLE,  "androidx.compose.material3", "material3"),

    ("biometric",              GOOGLE,  "androidx.biometric",      "biometric"),

    ("wearCompose",            GOOGLE,  "androidx.wear.compose",   "compose-material3"),
    ("wearComposeFoundation",  GOOGLE,  "androidx.wear.compose",   "compose-foundation"),
    ("wearComposeNavigation",  GOOGLE,  "androidx.wear.compose",   "compose-navigation"),
