    ("playServicesWearable",   GOOGLE,  "com.google.android.gms",  "play-services-wearable"),
    ("firebaseBom",            GOOGLE,  "com.google.firebase",     "firebase-bom"),
    ("mlkitBarcode",           GOOGLE,  "com.google.mlkit",        "barcode-scanning"),
    ("cameraX",                GOOGLE,  "androidx.camera",         "camera-camera2"),
    ("zxing",                  CENTRAL, "com.google.zxing",        "core"),
    ("junit",                  CENTRAL, "junit",                   "junit"),
    ("androidxTestExt",        GOOGLE,  "androidx.test.ext",       "junit"),
    ("espresso",               GOOGLE,  "androidx.test.espresso",  "espresso-core"),
]

UNSTABLE = re.compile(r"(alpha|beta|rc|dev|snapshot|-M\d|eap)", re.I)


def latest_stable(entry):
    label, repo, group, artifact = entry
    url = f"{repo}/{group.replace('.', '/')}/{artifact}/maven-metadata.xml"
    try:
        req = Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "curl/8"})
        with urlopen(req, timeout=25) as r:
            xml = r.read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
    except Exception as e:
        return label, None, f"{group}:{artifact}", f"FETCH-FAILED {e}"
    versions = re.findall(r"<version>([^<]+)</version>", xml)
    stable = [v for v in versions if not UNSTABLE.search(v)]
    if not stable:
        return label, None, f"{group}:{artifact}", "no stable version"

    def key(v):
        parts = []
        for p in re.split(r"[.\-+]", v):

        return parts

    try:

    except Exception:

    return label, best, f"{group}:{artifact}", "ok"

UNSTABLE = re.compile(r"(alpha|beta|rc|dev|snapshot|-M\d|eap)", re.I)


def latest_stable(entry):
    label, repo, group, artifact = entry
    url = f"{repo}/{group.replace('.', '/')}/{artifact}/maven-metadata.xml"
    try:
        req = Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "curl/8"})
        with urlopen(req, timeout=25) as r:

        for p in re.split(r"[.\-+]", v):

        return parts

    try:

    except Exception:

    return label, best, f"{group}:{artifact}", "ok"

<manifest xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android">

    <uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.type.watch" android:required="true" />

    <!-- The watch has no independent path to the desktop; everything arrives over the
         Data Layer from the phone. INTERNET is still needed by Play Services. -->
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.WAKE_LOCK" />
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />
    <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS" />

    <application
        android:allowBackup="false"
        android:fullBackupContent="false"
        android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher"
        android:label="@string/app_name"
        android:supportsRtl="true"
        android:theme="@android:style/Theme.DeviceDefault">

        <!-- Not standalone: this app is useless without the phone, which owns the only
             route to the desktop. Declaring standalone=true would let it install on a
             watch with no paired phone and then do nothing. -->
        <meta-data
            android:name="com.google.android.wearable.standalone"
            android:value="false" />

        <activity
            android:name=".MainActivity"
            android:exported="true"
            android:launchMode="singleTask"
            android:taskAffinity=""
            android:theme="@android:style/Theme.DeviceDefault">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>

        <service
            android:name=".datalayer.CompanionWearListenerService"
            android:exported="true">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="com.google.android.gms.wearable.DATA_CHANGED" />
                <action android:name="com.google.android.gms.wearable.MESSAGE_RECEIVED" />
                <data android:scheme="wear" android:host="*" />
            </intent-filter>
        </service>

    </application>

</manifest>

content.content:
Page doesn't contain the answer. It states what changed, not the new config syntax.

## What the page actually says

Built-in Kotlin: `android.builtInKotlin` flips `false` → `true` in AGP 9.0.

> "you no longer have to apply the `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` (or `kotlin-android`) plugin in your build files to compile Kotlin source files"

Incompatibility → hard requirement:

> "**Ensure your project is compatible with built-in Kotlin:** The `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` plugin is not compatible with the new DSL."

So: drop `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android`, apply nothing in its place. `com.android.application` / `com.android.library` handle Kotlin compilation.

KGP dependency: AGP 9.0 has runtime dep on KGP 2.2.10. Override version via top-level buildscript:

```
buildscript {
    dependencies {
        // For KGP
        classpath("org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-gradle-plugin:KGP_VERSION")

        // For KSP
        classpath("com.google.devtools.ksp:symbol-processing-gradle-plugin:KSP_VERSION")
    }
}
```

Only snippet on page touching Kotlin plugin config. Nothing about jvmTarget, compose, or serialization.

## Not covered — no snippets exist on this page

- jvmTarget / compilerOptions DSL location under built-in Kotlin
- Whether `org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose` / `.serialization` apply unchanged
- Any replacement compose/serialization config block

Two adjacent data points only:
- Java default source/target moved 8 → 11 ([Issue #369246556](https://issuetracker.google.com/issues/369246556)) — Java, not Kotlin `jvmTarget`
- kapt: `legacy-kapt` plugin exists; "Better exception when applying kapt plugin with built-in Kotlin" ([Issue #442763200](https://issuetracker.google.com/issues/442763200)). Implies compiler plugins need per-case handling. Doesn't say which.

I won't guess syntax here — wrong build config fails at configuration time and you'd be debugging my invention.

## Where to get it

1. [Migrate to built-in Kotlin](/build/migrate-to-built-in-kotlin) — linked repeatedly for this exact purpose. Also has `#opt-out-of-built-in-kotlin` and `#selectively-disable` anchors.
2. [AGP 9 upgrade skill](https://github.com/android/skills/tree/main/build/agp/agp-9-upgrade) (non-KMP)
3. [Gradle Recipes @ agp-9.0](https://github.com/android/gradle-recipes/tree/agp-9.0) — working build files
4. [AGP API reference](/reference/tools/gradle-api) — per-version API surface

## Escape hatch

Blocked on compose/serialization compat, opt out:

```
android.newDsl=false
```

Restores legacy DSL + old variant API; `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` works. Removed in AGP 10.0 (mid-2026). AGP 9.4 adds per-module opt-out.

Separate flag, separate concern — `android.builtInKotlin=false` opts out of built-in Kotlin only.

input.prompt: Show the exact build.gradle.kts configuration for AGP 9 built-in Kotlin. Specifically: (1) which plugins to apply for an Android app and library module using Kotlin, (2) how to set Kotlin jvmTarget and compilerOptions now, (3) whether org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose and org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.serialization are still applied as plugins or configured differently, (4) how to declare KSP. Quote exact code snippets.

content.content:
## 1. Plugins for app/library modules

Drop `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android`. AGP 9.0 enables built-in Kotlin by default.

```kotlin
// Module-level build file (app)
plugins {
    id("com.android.application")
}

// Module-level build file (library)
plugins {
    id("com.android.library")
}
```

Doc: "you no longer have to apply the `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android` (or `kotlin-android`) plugin in your build files to compile Kotlin source files."

Remove from top-level file too:

```kotlin
// Top-level build file — REMOVE
plugins {
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.android") version "KOTLIN_VERSION" apply false
}
```

And from `gradle/libs.versions.toml`:

```toml
[plugins]
kotlin-android = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.android", version.ref = "KOTLIN_VERSION" }
```

Not applying it → error:

```
Failed to apply plugin 'org.jetbrains.kotlin.android'.
    > Cannot add extension with name 'kotlin', as there is an extension already registered with that name.
```

## 2. jvmTarget / compilerOptions

`android.kotlinOptions{}` → `kotlin.compilerOptions{}`.

```kotlin
kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        languageVersion = org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.dsl.KotlinVersion.KOTLIN_2_0
        // Optional: Set jvmTarget
        // jvmTarget = org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.dsl.JvmTarget.JVM_11
    }
}
```

jvmTarget optional — doc: "you don't need to set `kotlin.compilerOptions.jvmTarget` because its value defaults to `android.compileOptions.targetCompatibility`."

## 3. Compose / serialization plugins

Page doesn't cover these. It scopes built-in Kotlin narrowly:

> "Built-in Kotlin replaces the `kotlin-android` plugin only."

Only other exception documented: KMP still needs `org.jetbrains.kotlin.multiplatform` + `com.android.kotlin.multiplatform.library`. No statement about compiler-plugin artifacts (`org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose`, `...plugin.serialization`) → assume still applied as plugins, but page is not authoritative. Verify against AGP 9.0 release notes.

## 4. KSP

Not covered on this page either. Only kapt is addressed:

> "The `org.jetbrains.kotlin.kapt` (or `kotlin-kapt`) plugin is incompatible with built-in Kotlin. If you use `kapt`, we recommend that you [migrate your project to KSP]."

Fallback if KSP migration not possible — swap to AGP-versioned kapt:

```toml
[plugins]
android-application = { id = "com.android.application", version.ref = "AGP_VERSION" }

# Add the following plugin definition
legacy-kapt = { id = "com.android.legacy-kapt", version.ref = "AGP_VERSION" }

# Remove the following plugin definition
kotlin-kapt = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.kapt", version.ref = "KOTLIN_VERSION" }
```

## Bonus: source dirs + opt-outs

Only supported source-dir API now:

```kotlin
# Add Kotlin source directories to AndroidSourceSet.kotlin
android.sourceSets.named("main") {
    kotlin.directories += "additionalSourceDirectory/kotlin"
}
```

Per-variant/generated:

```kotlin
androidComponents.onVariants { variant ->
    variant.sources.kotlin!!.addStaticSourceDirectory("additionalSourceDirectory/kotlin")
    variant.sources.kotlin!!.addGeneratedSourceDirectory(TASK_PROVIDER, TASK_OUTPUT)
}
```

Java-only module → skip Kotlin task + stdlib dep:

```kotlin
android {
    enableKotlin = false
}
```

Escape hatch (removed in AGP 10.0) — `gradle.properties`:

```
android.builtInKotlin=false
android.newDsl=false
```

Second line required: "the `kotlin-android` plugin is not compatible with it."

Module-by-module: set `android.builtInKotlin=false` globally, then apply `com.android.built-in-kotlin` (AGP version) per migrated module.

Known issues: [issuetracker.google.com/438678642](https://issuetracker.google.com/438678642).

No statement about compiler-plugin artifacts (`org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.compose`, `...plugin.serialization`) → assume still applied as plugins, but page is not authoritative. Verify against AGP 9.0 release notes.

## 4. KSP

Not covered on this page either. Only kapt is addressed:

> "The `org.jetbrains.kotlin.kapt` (or `kotlin-kapt`) plugin is incompatible with built-in Kotlin. If you use `kapt`, we recommend that you [migrate your project to KSP]."

Fallback if KSP migration not possible — swap to AGP-versioned kapt:

```toml
[plugins]
android-application = { id = "com.android.application", version.ref = "AGP_VERSION" }

# Add the following plugin definition
legacy-kapt = { id = "com.android.legacy-kapt", version.ref = "AGP_VERSION" }

# Remove the following plugin definition
kotlin-kapt = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.kapt", version.ref = "KOTLIN_VERSION" }
```

## Bonus: source dirs + opt-outs

Only supported source-dir API now:

```kotlin
# Add Kotlin source directories to AndroidSourceSet.kotlin
android.sourceSets.named("main") {
    kotlin.directories += "additionalSourceDirectory/kotlin"
}
```

Per-variant/generated:

```kotlin
androidComponents.onVariants { variant ->
    variant.sources.kotlin!!.addStaticSourceDirectory("additionalSourceDirectory/kotlin")
    variant.sources.kotlin!!.addGeneratedSourceDirectory(TASK_PROVIDER, TASK_OUTPUT)
}
```

Java-only module → skip Kotlin task + stdlib dep:

```kotlin
android {
    enableKotlin = false
}
```

Escape hatch (removed in AGP 10.0) — `gradle.properties`:

```
android.builtInKotlin=false
android.newDsl=false
```

Second line required: "the `kotlin-android` plugin is not compatible with it."

Module-by-module: set `android.builtInKotlin=false` globally, then apply `com.android.built-in-kotlin` (AGP version) per migrated module.

Known issues: [issuetracker.google.com/438678642](https://issuetracker.google.com/438678642).

const FINDINGS_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['blocker', 'high', 'medium', 'low'] },
          file: { type: 'string' },
          line: { type: 'integer' },
          title: { type: 'string' },
          detail: { type: 'string' },
          failure_scenario: { type: 'string' },
          fix: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['severity', 'file', 'title', 'detail', 'failure_scenario', 'fix'],
        additionalProperties: false,
      },
    },
  },
  required: ['findings'],
  additionalProperties: false,
}

const VERDICT_SCHEMA = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    real: { type: 'boolean' },
    reasoning: { type: 'string' },
    corrected_severity: { type: 'string', enum: ['blocker', 'high', 'medium', 'low', 'not-a-bug'] },
  },
  required: ['real', 'reasoning', 'corrected_severity'],
  additionalProperties: false,
}

const REVIEW_BASE = `${CONTEXT}

files — do not review from the reports alone. The reports below are for orientation only; they may
overstate what was done, and finding that discrepancy is itself a valid finding.

--- implementation reports ---
${buildReport}
--- end reports ---

You are an ADVERSARIAL reviewer. Find what is WRONG. A review that finds nothing is a failed review
unless you can demonstrate you looked hard. Read code, not comments. Every finding needs a CONCRETE
failure scenario: specific inputs or state leading to a specific wrong outcome. No style opinions, no
speculative refactors, no "consider adding a test". Defects only.
`

async function reviewRound(roundLabel, phaseName, lenses) {
  const raw = await pipeline(
    lenses,
    (l) => agent(`${REVIEW_BASE}\n\n## YOUR REVIEW LENS: ${l.key}\n\n${l.prompt}`,
      { label: `${roundLabel}:${l.key}`, phase: phaseName, model: 'opus', effort: 'xhigh', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA }),
    (res, lens) => {
      const items = (res && res.findings) ? res.findings : []
      if (!items.length) return []
      return parallel(items.map((f) => () =>
        agent(`${CONTEXT}

You are VERIFYING one review finding. DEFAULT TO REFUTING IT. Read the actual code at the cited
location and decide whether the defect is REAL.

NOT real if: the code already handles it elsewhere, the reviewer misread the control flow, it needs
state that cannot occur, it is a style preference, or it contradicts an explicit deliberate decision
in DESIGN.html. Deliberate accepted limitations are NOT bugs — including: no green dot; no offline
queueing; no certificate pinning; no retry on unconfirmed; the accepted pty-daemon queue race; the
accepted "bridge dies with the app" hole; Codex answering out of scope; enrichment layer cut from v1;
no Room/KSP; AGP 9 owning Kotlin compilation.

REAL if you can walk the actual code path and show the failure.

Lens: ${lens.key}
Claimed severity: ${f.severity}
File: ${f.file}${f.line ? ':' + f.line : ''}
Title: ${f.title}
Detail: ${f.detail}
Claimed failure scenario: ${f.failure_scenario}
Proposed fix: ${f.fix}`,
          { label: `verify:${(f.file || 'unknown').split('/').pop()}`, phase: phaseName, model: 'opus', effort: 'high', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA })
          .then((v) => ({ ...f, lens: lens.key, verdict: v }))
      ))
    }
  )
  const all = raw.filter(Boolean).flat().filter(Boolean)
  const confirmed = all.filter((f) => f.verdict && f.verdict.real && f.verdict.corrected_severity !== 'not-a-bug')
  log(`${roundLabel}: ${all.length} raw findings -> ${confirmed.length} confirmed after refutation`)
  return confirmed
}

function groupForRepair(findings) {
  const byArea = {}
  for (const f of findings) {
    const p = (f.file || '').replace(/\\/g, '/')
    let area = 'other'
    if (p.includes('/companion/')) area = 'bridge'
    else if (p.includes('apps/desktop/src/main')) area = 'desktop-main'
    else if (p.includes('app-watch')) area = 'client-watch'
    else if (p.includes('app-phone')) area = 'client-phone'
    else if (p.includes('/core/')) area = 'client-core'
    else if (p.includes('superset-companion')) area = 'client-other'
    else if (p.includes('fork-superset')) area = 'fork-other'
    if (!byArea[area]) byArea[area] = []
    byArea[area].push(f)
  }
  return Object.keys(byArea).map((k) => ({ area: k, items: byArea[k] }))
}

function repairPrompt(group, round) {
  const list = group.items.map((f, i) =>
    `${i + 1}. [${f.verdict.corrected_severity}] ${f.file}${f.line ? ':' + f.line : ''} — ${f.title}\n   ${f.detail}\n   FAILS WHEN: ${f.failure_scenario}\n   SUGGESTED FIX: ${f.fix}\n   VERIFIER: ${f.verdict.reasoning}`
  ).join('\n\n')
  return `${CONTEXT}

## REPAIR ROUND ${round} — area: ${group.area}

Every finding below survived refutation: an independent reviewer tried to disprove it and could not.
Fix each properly, in the real code.

 - Fix the ROOT CAUSE. No papering over symptoms, no catch that hides the failure, no weakening an
   assertion to make a problem disappear.
 - Edit only files in the '${group.area}' area from these findings, plus what is strictly required to
   make those fixes correct. Other agents repair other areas concurrently.
 - No state-changing git. No edits to FEATURES.md, any build file, or the version catalog.
 - If a finding is genuinely NOT a bug, or fixing it would violate an explicit design decision, say so
   explicitly — do not silently skip it.
 - If two findings conflict, resolve toward DESIGN.html and say so.

## FINDINGS (${group.items.length})

${list}

Report per finding: FIXED (file + what changed) or NOT-FIXED (why).
${RETURN_RULES}`
}

The first workflow failed and I've fixed the cause. Here's where things stand.

**What went wrong:** my own instruction. I told the scaffold agent to verify dependency versions with WebSearch rather than trust its training data. It took that literally, made 30 consecutive WebFetch calls enumerating Android library versions one at a time, and never reached the point of writing a file. 65 minutes, 842k tokens, zero output. Correct instinct, catastrophic execution order.

**What I did instead of retrying:** resolved all 40 versions myself in one batched query against Maven metadata — seconds, not an hour — then built the Gradle project by hand and *proved* it works rather than describing it:

- Both modules assemble in debug **and** release
- Both release APKs carry the identical certificate `b1ecb33b…`, matching the keystore exactly. That's the invariant the Wear Data Layer fails on silently, so it's now verified rather than assumed
- Committed as `79c4261`, local repo only — nothing near the fork or tonight's nightly, per your hold

Three things only compiling could have caught, all of which would have wrecked an agent working blind: AGP 9 compiles Kotlin itself now and rejects `kotlin.android` outright; `androidx.core` 1.19.0 demands compileSdk 37, and platforms are minor-versioned (`android-37.0`/`37.1`) so plain `37` doesn't exist as a package; and `local.properties` is a Java properties file, so single backslashes in a Windows path get eaten as escapes and resurface much later as an unrelated-looking `volume label syntax is incorrect`.

I also dropped Room and KSP. A read-through cache with nothing queued offline doesn't earn an annotation processor.

**Workflow v2 is running** with the stall class designed out: versions handed over as data with lookups forbidden, Gradle already green and off-limits to agents, no agent allowed to run Gradle at all (concurrent builds deadlock on file locks), and an explicit instruction to get files on disk early rather than researching first. Phase 0 is now two small bounded agents instead of one doing everything.

Still queued behind it, unchanged: 3× Codex `gpt-5.6-sol` at ultra, 3 Fable reviews, then `/simplify`.

20	 *
21	 * Error policy here, deliberate:
22	 *  * An **unknown path** is ignored with a warning. A newer phone build must be able to add
23	 *    a message type without bricking an older watch (PROTOCOL.md §0 forward compatibility).
24	 *  * An **undecodable payload on a known path** throws. That is not forward compatibility,
25	 *    it is the two sides disagreeing about a shape they both claim to implement, and it must
26	 *    be loud rather than producing a watch that quietly shows nothing.
27	 */
28	class CompanionWearListenerService : WearableListenerService() {
29	
30	    override fun onCreate() {
31	        super.onCreate()
32	        // Earliest hook this module owns. Does not cover install -> first launch; see
33	        // NotificationBridging for the two mechanisms that do.
34	        NotificationBridging.applyNoBridging(this)
35	    }
36	
37	    override fun onMessageReceived(event: MessageEvent) {
38	        val json = event.data.toString(Charsets.UTF_8)
39	        when (event.path) {
40	            WearPaths.QUESTION -> onQuestion(decode<WatchQuestion>(event.path, json))
41	            WearPaths.QUESTION_OVERSIZE -> onOversize(decode(event.path, json))
42	            WearPaths.QUESTION_RESOLVED -> onResolved(decode(event.path, json))
43	            WearPaths.ANSWER_RESULT -> onAnswerResult(decode(event.path, json))
44	            WearPaths.CONNECTION -> QuestionStore.onConnection(decode(event.path, json))
45	            else -> Log.w(TAG, "ignoring message on unknown path ${event.path}")
46	        }
47	    }
48	
49	    private fun onQuestion(question: WatchQuestion) {
50	        QuestionStore.onQuestion(question)
51	        val buzzed = QuestionNotifier.notifyQuestion(this, question)
52	        QuestionStore.setNotificationsBlocked(!buzzed)
53	    }
54	
55	    private fun onOversize(info: WatchQuestionOversize) {
56	        QuestionStore.onOversize(info)
57	        val buzzed = QuestionNotifier.notifyOversize(this, info)
58	        QuestionStore.setNotificationsBlocked(!buzzed)
59	    }
60	
61	    private fun onResolved(info: WatchQuestionResolved) {
62	        // A notification must never outlive the thing it was about (PROTOCOL.md §13.3) — cancel
63	        // first, unconditionally, whether or not the question is the one on screen.
64	        QuestionNotifier.cancel(this, info.questionId)
65	        QuestionStore.onResolved(info)
66	    }
67	
68	    private fun onAnswerResult(result: WatchAnswerResult) {
69	        QuestionStore.onAnswerResult(result)
70	        if (result.status == "confirmed") {
71	            QuestionNotifier.cancel(this, result.questionId)
72	        }
73	    }
74	
75	    private inline fun <reified T> decode(path: String, json: String): T =
76	        try {
77	            WearJson.decodeFromString<T>(json)
78	        } catch (e: SerializationException) {
79	            throw IllegalArgumentException(
80	                "undecodable ${T::class.java.simpleName} on $path (${json.length} chars)",
81	                e,
82	            )
83	        }
84	}

3	import android.app.Application

5	import family.khaira.supersetcompanion.phone.di.CompanionContainer
6	
7	/**
8	 * Process entry point.
9	 *
10	 * Two jobs, both deliberately tiny:
11	 *
12	 *  1. Build the dependency container eagerly so that a push arriving before any Activity
13	 *     exists (the normal case — the whole point of the product is answering a blocked
14	 *     agent while the phone is in a pocket) resolves the same singleton the UI will.
15	 *  2. Create the notification channels. Channels must exist before the first
16	 *     `notify()`, and the first `notify()` can come from
17	 *     [family.khaira.supersetcompanion.push.CompanionMessagingService] with no Activity
18	 *     in the process.
19	 *
20	 * There is no network call here, no key unwrap, and no disk scan. Startup work that
21	 * blocks is how the desktop fork already learned this lesson the hard way; the phone gets
22	 * the same rule.
23	 */
24	class SupersetCompanionApp : Application() {
25	
26	    override fun onCreate() {
27	        super.onCreate()
28	        val container = CompanionContainer.get(this)
29	        container.notifications.ensureChannels()
30	        if (container.repository.isFake) {
31	            // Loud on purpose. Fake mode is a legitimate, useful state — it is how every
32	            // screen is developed and how every failure path stays reachable — but it must
33	            // never be mistaken for a real desktop, so it announces itself.
34	            Log.w(TAG, "FAKE DATA MODE: no bridge is contacted; every screen is fabricated.")
35	        }
36	    }
37	
38	    private companion object {
39	        const val TAG = "SupersetCompanion"
40	    }
41	}

28	    /** Rejected at the edge — service token missing, wrong, or revoked. */
29	    data class AccessDenied(val detail: String) : ConnectionState
30	
31	    /** No usable network on this device. */
32	    data object Offline : ConnectionState
33	
34	    /** Reached something, but it was not a shape we understand. */
35	    data class Unexpected(val status: Int, val detail: String) : ConnectionState
36	
37	    // --- The rest of the PROTOCOL.md §8 taxonomy -----------------------------
38	    // Added alongside the four states that were confirmed against the live tunnel.
39	    // They are separate members for the same reason those four are: each one sends the
40	    // user somewhere different, and merging any two of them wastes a trip to the desk.
41	
42	    /**
43	     * `401 unknown_device` or `401 not_paired`. The key this phone holds is not one the
44	     * bridge knows — or the GCM tag failed, which the bridge deliberately reports
45	     * identically. Either way the fix is to pair again.
46	     */
47	    data object Unpaired : ConnectionState
48	
49	    /**
50	     * `403 access_denied` with a **sealed** `reason: "revoked"`. Distinct from
51	     * [AccessDenied], which is the edge refusing us: here the bridge knows exactly who we
52	     * are and has withdrawn permission, so the device can still say why it stopped.
53	     */
54	    data class Revoked(val reason: String) : ConnectionState
55	
56	    /**
57	     * TLS handshake failure. Never retried silently — certificate pinning is deliberately
58	     * not used (Cloudflare rotates certs on a ~90-day cycle and controls its issuing CAs),
59	     * so a handshake failure here is a real anomaly rather than an expected rotation.
60	     */
61	    data class TlsFailed(val detail: String) : ConnectionState
62	
63	    /** Connect or read timeout. The desktop did not respond in time. */
64	    data object Timeout : ConnectionState
65	
66	    /** `503 bridge_unavailable`: Superset is starting, or shutting down. Retry with backoff. */
67	    data object BridgeStarting : ConnectionState
68	
69	    /**
70	     * `503 edge_unverifiable`: the bridge could not fetch the Cloudflare Access JWKS and
71	     * **failed closed** rather than trusting the header. Retry with backoff.
72	     */
73	    data object EdgeUnverifiable : ConnectionState
74	}

**Companion repo:** `PROTOCOL.md` at 80KB, 79 Kotlin files across `core/`, `app-phone/`, `app-watch/`.

- Bridge: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/fork-superset-windows-arm64/packages/host-service/src/companion/`
  Your files: `answer.ts` (guard stack), `keystrokes.ts` (byte encoder), `lease.ts`, `question-store.ts`, `index.ts` (guard adapters), `audit.ts`
- Contract: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/PROTOCOL.md` §11
- Rationale: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/DESIGN.html`

# The byte contract — PROVEN EMPIRICALLY, do not re-derive, verify the code MATCHES it

Established by driving the real Claude Code CLI 2.1.220 in a pty across scripted runs:

- **Single-select: ONE bare digit both selects AND submits.** No Enter. No confirmation step. Atomic.
- **Several questions in one call:** N digits, then `\r` on the review screen.
- **multiSelect INVERTS the rules:** digits and space TOGGLE; **Enter TOGGLES and does NOT submit**; submitting is right-arrow `\x1b[C` to the Submit tab, then `\r`. A naive implementation that appends Enter to "submit" silently flips a selection.
- **Free text:** digit N+1 opens an inline editor, then UTF-8, then `\r`.
- **Bracketed paste is INERT against the picker.** `terminal.send` / `writeFramedInputToSession` cannot drive it. Only raw `terminal.writeInput` works.

Stale bytes are the core hazard: with the picker gone, digits land in the composer and a following Enter submits them as a real prompt (observed: a stray `23` became a genuine prompt the model burned a turn on). Mid-turn, input queues and steers the running agent. Against a *different* picker, a digit commits instantly against the wrong question. **Because digits commit atomically there is no safe retry.**

# The six guards — all must pass, as ONE transaction, not a checklist

1. The question's `tool_use_id` still has NO `tool_result` in the transcript.
2. The agent-session binding still matches (a `/resume` or restart invalidates it).
3. The terminal session is still active.
4. The permission axis is still latched.
5. A snapshot confirms the picker is still on screen showing THAT question.
6. The `.askq` marker still exists — worthless as proof, but its ABSENCE is a sound veto.

**Guards 2 and 4 are FORGEABLE**: they read a store written by `notifications.hook`, which is deliberately unauthenticated on localhost and whose URL sits in every agent shell's environment. So an agent that reads attacker-controlled content can forge them. Guards 1 and 5 are the load-bearing ones. Round 2 already found that guard 5 was matching anchors the attacker supplies, and that guard 1 read a file path the unauthenticated hook chose. **Assume more of this class remains.**

# The lease

Locking per keystroke is insufficient and the reason is counter-intuitive: multiSelect digits TOGGLE, so phone `{1,2}` against watch `{1,3}`, perfectly serialised, interleaves into `{2,3}` — an answer NEITHER device chose, with every guard passing before every byte. One answer holds one lease for its whole sequence; a second device is REFUSED, never queued.

# What to do

1. **Test the encoder exhaustively.** `keystrokes.ts` is pure and directly testable. Drive it with bun/node. Enumerate single-select, multi-question, multiSelect (including the submit shape), and free text. Assert the exact byte sequences against the contract above. Property-test it: does any input produce a trailing `\r` after a multiSelect toggle? Any path emitting bytes for a Codex terminal? Any path reaching `terminal.send` instead of `writeInput`?
2. **Attack the guard stack.** For each guard, ask: what does it ACTUALLY read, who can write that, and does a hostile value pass? Trace the adapters in `index.ts` — that is where round 2 found the real holes. Specifically probe whether guard 5's screen match can be satisfied by attacker-chosen text, and whether guard 1 can be pointed at a file the attacker controls or an empty one.
3. **Attack the transaction boundary.** Is the read-verify-write genuinely under one lock, or can the screen change between check and byte? Is there ANY path that writes without the full stack? Any partial-write path leaving a question re-answerable, so a multiSelect gets re-toggled?
4. **Attack the lease.** Concurrency-test it. Two simultaneous answers, same question. Answer during a lease TTL expiry. Re-pair mid-lease. Crash mid-sequence. Does `unconfirmed` ever become a retry?
5. **Audit log**: written BEFORE execution? Forgeable? Truncatable? Missing events?

# Rules

input.prompt:
You are reviewing an Android + Wear OS companion app and its desktop bridge, all written by AI agents in one pass. Your lens is **would this actually work for the person using it?** Not "is the code correct in the abstract" — does the real end-to-end journey hold together.

# The product

The user runs many AI coding agents in terminal panes on a Windows desktop. Agents block for hours waiting on a question while the user is away from the machine. `superset-companion` carries that to their phone and watch and lets them answer from the wrist.

Measured over 7 real days: 300 blocking questions, 97.7% answerable remotely, median question 1,412 characters with **64% over the 1,024-char Android notification clamp**, 59% of prompts contain several questions, ~10% multiSelect.

Repos:
- Desktop bridge: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/fork-superset-windows-arm64/packages/host-service/src/companion/`, keep-awake at `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/keep-awake/`, hook capture in `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/agent-jsonl-watcher/pane-map-hook.ts` and `packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/`
- Android: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/` — `core/`, `app-phone/`, `app-watch/`
- **Read first**: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/DESIGN.html` (the product decisions and why), then `PROTOCOL.md` (the wire contract), then `SETUP.md` (what infrastructure really exists)

# YOUR ASSIGNMENT: trace complete journeys end to end, through the real code

For each journey below, follow the ACTUAL code across both repos — desktop hook, bridge, transport, phone, Data Layer, watch — and find where it breaks, stalls, lies to the user, or produces a state no screen explains.

**J1 — the core loop.** An agent raises an AskUserQuestion. The PreToolUse hook fires and forwards the payload. Three minutes pass with nobody answering at the desk. A push goes out. The phone is dozing in a pocket. The user feels the watch buzz, reads the whole question, taps an option. The bridge verifies and injects. The agent continues.
Walk every hop. Does the question text survive intact? Does the delayed push actually arm, and does the awake-credit sweep suppress it correctly when the user IS at the desk? Does the watch get the full text rather than a truncated bridged copy? Does the answer reach a real terminal? Does the user see confirmation?

**J2 — the multi-question case, which is 59% of real questions.** A prompt with three questions arrives. Does the phone render all three? Does the watch? Can the user answer them all from the wrist, and does partial progress behave sanely if they put the watch down halfway?

**J3 — answered at the desk first.** The user answers at the keyboard while the phone notification is already showing. Does the notification retract everywhere, including on a watch that was asleep? Does the phone sheet close or explain itself? Is there any window where the phone would inject a second answer?

**J4 — both devices at once.** The user opens the question on the phone and the watch. One holds the lease. What does the OTHER device actually show? Is the refusal legible, or does it look like a bug?

**J5 — the unhappy paths, as experienced.** Desktop asleep (530). Superset closed but desktop awake (502). Access credential wrong (403). Phone offline. Bridge dies mid-answer. Answer times out unconfirmed. For each: what does the user SEE, and does it tell them the right thing to do? The design is explicit that "desktop asleep" and "Superset not running" must be distinguishable, because otherwise the user goes and pokes a machine that was fine.

**J6 — first run.** Install both APKs, launch the phone app, scan the QR, pair. Does the flow actually work as coded — including the LAN pairing hop, which requires phone and desktop on the same network? Is that requirement communicated anywhere? What happens on the watch between installing it and first launching it (the design flags this window as the most likely thing to be wrong)?

**J7 — the Fold.** Home and chat share one adaptive scaffold. Open a question on the cover screen, unfold. Does selection survive? Fold back mid-answer?

# Also judge, as a product

- **Notification volume.** The 3-minute delay exists because ~50 buzzes a day gets the watch muted within a week, and muted equals not built. Does the implementation actually deliver that, including retraction and the foreground sweep?
- **Honesty of state.** The design insists every answer shows pending / confirmed / failed and never collapses to "sent", because an unconfirmed answer is a real distinct outcome that is never retried. Is that honoured everywhere, on both devices?
- **Anything that would silently do nothing.** The worst failure mode here is not a crash — it is a surface that appears to work and quietly does not, because the user then trusts it while agents sit blocked.

# Rules

- Read the ACTUAL code, both repos. Do not infer from documentation.
- DELIBERATE, not defects: no green status dot (only red/yellow/neutral); no snooze/archive/pin mirroring; nothing queues offline; no certificate pinning; no retry on unconfirmed; Codex terminals unanswerable in v1; the bridge dies with the desktop app; multi-select and free text are last in the build order.
- Do NOT modify any file. Do NOT run state-changing git commands. Review only — other reviewers are in these repos concurrently.
- Never print a secret value.

# Output

Organise by journey. For each break: severity, exact file and line, what the user experiences, and the fix. Call out separately anything that would **silently do nothing**. End with your judgement of whether this would actually be usable on day one, and the single change that would most improve it.

You are reviewing a large AI-written change set that is about to be committed into a **vendored fork that survives on automated nightly merges from upstream**. Your lens is: **what does this change do to the fork, and is the risk surface justified?**

# Context

`superset-companion` adds an internet-exposed bridge to the desktop app that answers a blocked AI agent's terminal question by injecting keystrokes. The desktop half lands inside a fork of `superset-sh/superset` that merges upstream nightly through deterministic gates plus an unattended AI repair loop.

**Read first**: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/fork-superset-windows-arm64/AGENTS.md` — the fork's architecture, non-negotiables and live footguns. Then `FEATURES.md` and `scripts/ci-repair.sh`.

The change set (`git status --short`, do NOT commit):
```
 M FEATURES.md
 M apps/desktop/src/main/lib/agent-jsonl-watcher/pane-map-hook.ts
 M apps/desktop/src/main/windows/main.ts
 M packages/host-service/src/app.ts
 M packages/host-service/src/serve.ts
 M packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/index.ts
 M packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/notifications.ts
 M packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/router.ts
 M scripts/ci-repair.sh
?? apps/desktop/src/main/lib/keep-awake/
?? packages/host-service/src/companion/            (18 files)
?? packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/companion/
?? packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/companion-question-sink.ts
```

Design rationale lives at `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/DESIGN.html`; the wire contract at `PROTOCOL.md` (1,754 lines).

# YOUR ASSIGNMENT — three parts

## Part 1: merge survival

Every line added to an UPSTREAM-OWNED file is permanent merge burden, forever. Audit each modified upstream file and judge:
- Is the seam as small as it can be, or is fork logic living where upstream owns the file? One review already found 142 lines of fork business logic authored inside an upstream router — check whether that was actually moved out.
- Are calls into upstream internals funnelled through ONE adapter, so an upstream rename breaks in one visible place rather than many invisible ones?
- Does every `FEATURES.md` marker token literally appear in code under its declared path? A marker that does not is a gate failure; a seam with no marker is a feature that a clean merge can silently delete. One review found all three markers satisfied only by fork-only files, leaving every upstream seam unguarded — verify that is fixed.
- `pane-map-hook.ts` carries an EMBEDDED PYTHON TEMPLATE. Two known traps: backticks anywhere in it break the esbuild template, and reading its stdin in text mode has previously cp1252-mojibaked non-ASCII content. Check both. Also confirm the existing agent status-dot behaviour is strictly unchanged — that edit must be purely additive, and regressing the dots is a hard failure.
- Does anything assert an upstream-derived INCIDENTAL name (chunk filenames, hashes, ordering)? That class of mistake has already blocked three consecutive nightlies.

## Part 2: the `ci-repair.sh` edit

`scripts/ci-repair.sh` is the fork's unattended BUILD-REPAIR engine and is ITSELF a frozen gate script. An agent modified it to add `packages/host-service/src/companion` to `FROZEN_GATE_PATHS`, implementing a DESIGN.html recommendation: this code is internet-exposed, holds credentials, and can type into terminals, so an unattended repair agent reading a build log an attacker may have influenced must not be able to edit it.

Verify precisely:
- Does the added path ACTUALLY freeze the whole subtree given how `git diff -- <pathspec>` is used there?
- Does the freeze cover everything it should? What about `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/keep-awake/`, `trpc/router/companion/`, `companion-question-sink.ts`, and the upstream seams?
- Does freezing MORE paths create a new failure mode — can a legitimate build break now become unrepairable in a way that hard-fails every nightly rather than failing loud once?
- Is the edit consistent with the rest of the script's logic and its diagnosis-file escape hatch?

## Part 3: is the risk surface justified?

This is the part only a human-quality judgement can do. The change is ~19,000 lines across two repos, an 18-file bridge, and a 1,754-line protocol — for a single-user personal app.

- What here is genuinely load-bearing, and what is over-built? Be specific and name files.
- Where does complexity itself create risk — code that exists mainly to serve other code, abstractions with one implementation, protocol features nothing uses?
- The design deliberately CUT an enrichment layer and rejected the ACP path to keep scope down. Judge whether the result still respects that discipline.
- Is there anything you would simply delete?

Be concrete. A later pass will act on this, so name the file and say what should go.

# Rules

- Read the ACTUAL code. Use `git diff` (read-only) to see exactly what changed in modified files.
- DELIBERATE, not defects: no certificate pinning; no offline queueing; no retry on unconfirmed; the accepted pty-daemon queue race; the bridge dying with the desktop app; no green status dot; Codex unanswerable in v1; no Room/KSP.
- Do NOT modify any file. Do NOT run state-changing git commands. Other reviewers are working in these repos concurrently.
- Never print a secret value.

# Output

Three sections matching the parts above. Per finding: severity, exact file and line, the concrete consequence (especially "which nightly does this break, and how"), and the fix. End with: would you commit this to the fork as it stands, and if not, what is the minimum that must change first.

Status while things run:

**Workflow done** — 137 agents, 15.5M tokens, 2.7 hours, zero failures. It found real bugs, which is the point. Two rounds surfaced 103 raw findings; each went to an independent reviewer instructed to *refute* it, and 71 survived and were fixed.

The ones that matter tell you how necessary this was:

- The phone had **no Wear listener at all**. `sendMessage` resolves on delivery to the node, not on a listener existing — so every watch answer returned success into a void and the watch sat on "Unconfirmed" forever. The entire watch surface was inert with no error anywhere.
- Bridge and client derived **different keys** — HKDF `info` was base64url text on one side, raw bytes on the other. Nothing would have decrypted and nothing would have said why.
- Guard 5 matched anchors the *caller* supplies, so a forged capture with one-character labels passed against a terminal with no picker open. That's the guard standing between a forged localhost POST and keystrokes in a live terminal.
- The question sink was never registered, so captured questions never reached the store and every answer returned 410.

All gates green afterwards: both APKs build debug and release, identical signing certificate, 82/82 feature markers present, REFERR clean, keep-awake tests 17/17, and zero new TypeScript errors (desktop diagnostics actually went 34 → 33).

Committed to the companion repo as `913ec60`. Fork side stays uncommitted per your hold.

**Codex hit a snag worth flagging:** its safety classifier refused the first run — my prompts asked it to "attack the unauthenticated surface" and "flood it", which reads as offensive security regardless of it being your own machine. I've rewritten that one as what it actually is, an input-validation and resource-bounds review, and relaunched. The other two are still running and may hit the same wall; I'll rephrase those the same way if so.

**Three Fable reviewers are running concurrently** on angles the workflow couldn't cover: whether the 71 repairs actually fixed things or just moved them, whether the end-to-end journeys hold up as a product, and what the change does to the fork's nightly merge — plus what should simply be deleted, which feeds `/simplify`.

I am the author of this personal project and I am asking you to review and test its most safety-critical component before I rely on it. It was written quickly by AI agents. Please write and run real tests — a finding demonstrated by execution is worth ten reasoned about.

# What it does

I run AI coding agents in terminal panes on my desktop. When one asks me a multiple-choice question it blocks until I answer. This feature lets me answer from my phone or watch: a small service inside my desktop app sends the same keystrokes to the terminal that my fingers would.

The risk is entirely about **timing and correctness**, not about anyone else's machine. If the service sends keystrokes when the question is no longer on screen, those characters land somewhere else — into a composer where they become a real prompt, or against a different question where they immediately commit the wrong choice. There is no undo. So the code has to be certain the right question is still displayed before it sends anything.

# Where the code is

- `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/fork-superset-windows-arm64/packages/host-service/src/companion/`
  - `keystrokes.ts` — the byte encoder (pure, directly testable)
  - `answer.ts` — the precondition checks and the send sequence
  - `lease.ts` — the mutual-exclusion lease
  - `question-store.ts` — where pending questions are held
  - `index.ts` — the adapters that supply each precondition check with its data
  - `audit.ts` — the write log
- Contract: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/PROTOCOL.md` §11
- Rationale: `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/DESIGN.html`

Package manager is `bun`, not npm.

# The keystroke contract — established empirically, verify the code MATCHES it

I measured this by driving the real Claude Code CLI 2.1.220 inside a pty. Do not re-derive it; check the implementation against it:

- **Single-select: one bare digit both selects AND submits.** No Enter. No confirmation step. It is atomic.
- **Several questions in one prompt:** N digits, then `\r` on the review screen.
- **Multi-select inverts the rules:** digits and space TOGGLE a choice; **Enter also toggles and does NOT submit**; submitting is right-arrow `\x1b[C` to reach the Submit tab, then `\r`. An implementation that appends Enter to "submit" silently flips a selection instead.
- **Free text:** digit N+1 opens an inline editor, then UTF-8 text, then `\r`.
- **Bracketed-paste framing is inert here.** The wrapped form produces cursor noise and no state change, so the framed write helper cannot drive this UI at all — only the raw write path works.

Because a digit commits atomically, **there is no safe retry**. A repeat can commit against a different question that has since opened.

# What I would like you to do

## 1. Test the encoder exhaustively — highest value, and completely self-contained

`keystrokes.ts` is a pure function. Drive it directly with bun or node and assert exact byte sequences against the contract above. Enumerate single-select, several-questions-in-one-prompt, multi-select (especially the submit shape), and free text.

Then property-test it. Does any input produce a trailing `\r` after a multi-select toggle? Does any path emit bytes for a terminal type that is out of scope (Codex terminals are excluded in v1 because the contract was measured against Claude Code and does not generalise)? Does any path reach the framed write helper instead of the raw one? Does a question whose `multiSelect` flag disagrees with the answer shape produce output rather than a refusal?

## 2. Review the precondition checks for trust-boundary correctness

Before sending anything, `answer.ts` requires six conditions. Two of them read a store populated by a local hook endpoint that is deliberately unauthenticated on loopback and whose URL sits in every agent's environment — so **any local process can write to it**, and those two conditions therefore cannot be relied upon. The two that are meant to be authoritative are the transcript check (has this question already been answered?) and the screen check (is this exact question still displayed?).

An earlier review found the screen check was matching text that the same untrusted store supplied — so a record with one-character labels satisfied it against a terminal displaying nothing. It also found the transcript check reading a file path chosen by that same store.

Please trace, in the current code, the actual data flow from that hook endpoint through to each of the six conditions, and tell me whether either authoritative check still depends on data the untrusted store controls. This is the single thing I most want checked.

## 3. Check the send is atomic with the checks

Evaluating conditions and then sending are two separate acts unless they are held under one lock — everything can pass and the display can still change before the bytes land. Verify the read, the evaluation and the write genuinely happen under a single lock, and that no code path sends without the full set. Look for partial-send paths that leave a question re-answerable, since re-answering a multi-select re-toggles it into a combination nobody chose.

## 4. Test the lease under concurrency

Locking per keystroke is not enough, for a reason worth stating: multi-select digits toggle, so if my phone answers `{1,2}` while my watch answers `{1,3}`, perfectly serialised keystrokes interleave into `{2,3}` — a combination neither device chose, with every condition passing before every byte. One answer must hold one lease for its whole sequence, and a second device must be refused outright rather than queued.

Test it: two simultaneous answers to one question; an answer arriving as the lease TTL expires; re-pairing mid-lease; a crash mid-sequence. Confirm that an "unconfirmed" outcome never turns into a retry.

## 5. The audit log

Is each write appended BEFORE it executes? Can entries be lost, truncated, or silently skipped?

# Constraints

- These are deliberate decisions, not defects: no retry on an unconfirmed send; the accepted race where a keypress I make at the desk is already queued in the pty daemon and beats any lock the service holds; Codex terminals out of scope in v1; the service exiting with the desktop app; nothing queued while offline.
- Scratch files under `fork-superset-windows-arm64/tmp/` are fine. Do not modify production source, do not run state-changing git commands, do not edit build files.
- **Do not send keystrokes to any of my real running agent terminals.** Test the encoder and the checks in isolation.
- Do not print credential values.

# Output

Per finding: severity, exact file and line, what is wrong, a concrete scenario in which it produces the wrong outcome, **the test you ran and its actual output**, and the fix. End with what you tested, what you could not, and your single strongest objection to the design.

content.text:
The `ci-repair.sh` edit is sound. It adds the companion directory to `FROZEN_GATE_PATHS`, and since the check uses `git diff -- <pathspec>`, a directory entry does cover the whole subtree. The reasoning in the comment is right too: nothing in that loop reviews a repair for semantic correctness, and the build log the agent reads is untrusted, so an agent "fixing" a type error by coercing an unreadable guard's `null` to `true` would pass every deterministic gate and ship.

But I found a gap it misses. Three parts of the same trust surface sit **outside** the frozen path:

- `packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/notifications/companion-question-sink.ts` — this feeds the question store, which feeds the guards
- `packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/companion/` — exposes pairing and the panic switch
- `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/keep-awake/`

So an unattended repair agent still can't touch the guard stack, but it *can* edit the thing that supplies the guards their data. That's most of the way to the same outcome. I'll fold it into the fix batch once the reviewers report — `fable-fork` was asked this specific question, so I'll take its answer alongside mine rather than pre-empting it.

content.text:
Verified — the finding is real, but I disagree with its proposed fix, and the disagreement matters.

Confirmed: `handleAnswerStatus` returns `record.status` raw, which can be `"in_flight"`. The Kotlin `AnswerStatusValue` enum has no such member, its serializer falls back to `UNKNOWN`, and `BridgeCompanionRepository`'s `else` branch turns that into `AnswerOutcome.Failed(INTERNAL, "…this build does not understand")`. So polling during the injection window shows a **terminal failure for an answer that is actually landing**.

The reviewer wants `in_flight` mapped to `unconfirmed` on the wire. But the bridge's own comment at `types.ts:856` explicitly refuses that, and it has a point — during injection the answer *is* actively landing, which is genuinely different from "outcome unknown."

The deeper defect is the client's fallback: an **unrecognised** status becomes a terminal `Failed`. That's "fail fast and loud" misapplied. Reporting *failed* when you don't know isn't loud, it's wrong — and it's wrong in the direction that makes the user re-answer a question that already succeeded. An unknown status should degrade to non-terminal `Unconfirmed`, which is honest and pollable. That also fixes the forward-compat case the reviewer didn't consider: any older client build meeting a newer bridge hits the same false-failure path for any status added later.

So the fix is: add `in_flight` to PROTOCOL §11.5 and the client enum mapping to the pending UI state, **and** make the unrecognised-status fallback non-terminal.

I'm holding it for a single consolidated batch rather than applying it now — four reviewers are still reading this exact code and I don't want them reporting against a moving target.

Everything else in that review came back clean: all 18 verified blocker/high fixes were genuine root-cause fixes, not suppressed symptoms. The two crypto-interop blockers were resolved by adopting one documented convention on *both* runtimes, with a cross-runtime differential test left behind as a drift tripwire — which is the outcome you want from a repair rather than a patch.

75:| Companion keep-awake | the phone/watch companion is worthless if the desktop sleeps mid-question: the answer path lives in host-service, which dies with the machine. The main process holds a power-save blocker (and suppresses app-initiated sleep) for exactly as long as the companion bridge is enabled AND at least one device is paired, released the moment either stops being true — it never pins the machine awake unconditionally, and it never blocks display sleep (screen off is fine; suspend is not) | `(KEEP-AWAKE)` |
76:| Companion question capture | the `PreToolUse` AskUserQuestion hook payload already carries everything needed to DISCOVER and render a blocking question — `tool_name`, `tool_use_id`, `transcript_path`, `session_id`, `cwd`, `tool_input.questions[]` (`question`/`header`/`multiSelect`/`options[]`) plus `agent_id`/`agent_type` when a subagent asked — so the capture path forwards it to the bridge's question store instead of parsing transcripts (measured: 300 blocking questions over 7 days, 97.7% answerable, median 1 412 chars, 59% multi-question, ~10% multiSelect). Question text is captured VERBATIM and never truncated: a question longer than the terminal window was never retained in scrollback, so the screen can verify a picker but can never be its source | `(COMPANION-CAPTURE)` |
77:| Companion bridge (phone/watch) | fork-only host-service subsystem (`packages/host-service/src/companion/`) that lets a paired Android phone/watch read agent status and answer a blocked AskUserQuestion. Loopback listener on a fixed port behind a Cloudflare tunnel + Access service token, with the bridge validating the Access JWT itself and failing closed; every body is an end-to-end AES-256-GCM sealed envelope keyed on a per-device key that is DERIVED at pairing and never transmitted, with method/path/status/nonce bound into the AAD and a disk-persisted replay cache that outlives the freshness window. The client sends semantic intent only — questionId, fingerprint, option indices — so no wire field can express "send these bytes to that terminal"; the bridge owns the picker byte contract, evaluates its six guards and injects inside ONE critical section holding the per-terminal lock in the same process as the pty writer, under an answer-wide lease (per-keystroke locking interleaves two multi-select answers into a third one neither device chose). First-answer-wins, zero write retries, read-the-outcome instead. Push is data-only opaque ids with runtime assertions that make text leakage throw, delayed 3 min so only genuinely-unattended questions buzz. Wire contract: `superset-companion/PROTOCOL.md` | `(COMPANION-BRIDGE)` |

75:| Companion keep-awake | the phone/watch companion is worthless if the desktop sleeps mid-question: the answer path lives in host-service, which dies with the machine. The main process holds a power-save blocker (and suppresses app-initiated sleep) for exactly as long as the companion bridge is enabled AND at least one device is paired, released the moment either stops being true — it never pins the machine awake unconditionally, and it never blocks display sleep (screen off is fine; suspend is not) | `(KEEP-AWAKE)` |
76:| Companion question capture | the `PreToolUse` AskUserQuestion hook payload already carries everything needed to DISCOVER and render a blocking question — `tool_name`, `tool_use_id`, `transcript_path`, `session_id`, `cwd`, `tool_input.questions[]` (`question`/`header`/`multiSelect`/`options[]`) plus `agent_id`/`agent_type` when a subagent asked — so the capture path forwards it to the bridge's question store instead of parsing transcripts (measured: 300 blocking questions over 7 days, 97.7% answerable, median 1 412 chars, 59% multi-question, ~10% multiSelect). Question text is captured VERBATIM and never truncated: a question longer than the terminal window was never retained in scrollback, so the screen can verify a picker but can never be its source | `(COMPANION-CAPTURE)` |
77:| Companion bridge (phone/watch) | fork-only host-service subsystem (`packages/host-service/src/companion/`) that lets a paired Android phone/watch read agent status and answer a blocked AskUserQuestion. Loopback listener on a fixed port behind a Cloudflare tunnel + Access service token, with the bridge validating the Access JWT itself and failing closed; every body is an end-to-end AES-256-GCM sealed envelope keyed on a per-device key that is DERIVED at pairing and never transmitted, with method/path/status/nonce bound into the AAD and a disk-persisted replay cache that outlives the freshness window. The client sends semantic intent only — questionId, fingerprint, option indices — so no wire field can express "send these bytes to that terminal"; the bridge owns the picker byte contract, evaluates its six guards and injects inside ONE critical section holding the per-terminal lock in the same process as the pty writer, under an answer-wide lease (per-keystroke locking interleaves two multi-select answers into a third one neither device chose). First-answer-wins, zero write retries, read-the-outcome instead. Push is data-only opaque ids with runtime assertions that make text leakage throw, delayed 3 min so only genuinely-unattended questions buzz. Wire contract: `superset-companion/PROTOCOL.md` | `(COMPANION-BRIDGE)` |

The complete report includes, for every finding, exact production lines, failure scenario, executed command, actual output, and proposed fix:

### Most serious findings

- **Critical:** Android re-pairing clears/reinitializes the nonce counter before committing the new pairing record. A crash in between reused old K_dev + old prefix + counter 1001 exactly.
- **Critical:** Restoring an older counter repeats exact AES-GCM nonces on both runtimes: bridge counter 65537 and Android counter 1001 reproduced identically.

- **High:** A forward clock jump and correction purges replay records, then admits the captured request again.
- **High:** The complete QR URI—including the 256-bit pairing code—is deliberately written to logs despite a protocol MUST NOT.
- **High:** Restoring an old `devices.json` reverses revocation while retained K_dev makes terminal writes valid again.

Additional demonstrated defects cover unauthenticated KEX metadata mutation, KEX replay exhaustion, JWKS rollback, Windows ACL drift, orphaned keys after purge failure, corrupt nonce state failing open, Android base64url alias acceptance, missing key zeroization, unbounded JWKS body buffering, and a device-existence timing oracle.

### Compatibility result

The runtimes matched on:

- Every HKDF salt, info string, length, and output
- 39-byte header layout and offsets
- Request, response, event, and pairing AAD
- Pairing transcript and its hash
- Nonce prefix/counter encoding
- Complete AES-GCM ciphertexts and tags
- Bidirectional cross-opening of all envelope forms
- Dynamic X25519 and the RFC 7748 vector

The sole differential mismatch was Android accepting non-canonical base64url tail bits. The full runner exits 1 intentionally on that regression test; the canonical-only JVM test passes.

Test artifacts include the [differential runner](<C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/fork-superset-windows-arm64/tmp/differential_vectors/run-differential.ps1>) and [JVM compatibility test](<C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/superset-companion/core/src/test/java/family/khaira/supersetcompanion/core/crypto/CrossRuntimeDifferentialVectors20260729Test.kt>).

My strongest objection is architectural: nonce, replay, and revocation authority is split across independently rollbackable flat files without a transaction or anti-rollback anchor. The tests prove that filesystem history moving backward can both destroy AES-GCM nonce uniqueness and reactivate revoked terminal-write capability.

I have a small pure TypeScript function that needs thorough unit tests, and I would like you to write and run them. There is no framework preference — driving it directly with `bun` and asserting is fine.

# The function

`C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/fork-superset-windows-arm64/packages/host-service/src/companion/keystrokes.ts`

It converts a chosen answer into the exact key presses a person would type into a command-line tool's interactive multiple-choice prompt. Its output is a byte sequence. Package manager here is **bun**, not npm.

# The specification it must match

I established this by driving the real CLI (Claude Code 2.1.220) inside a pseudo-terminal and recording what each key press did. Please treat it as ground truth and check the implementation against it:

- **Single choice: one bare digit both selects and confirms.** There is no Enter and no confirmation step — the prompt closes on the digit alone.
- **Several questions in one prompt:** one digit per question, then a carriage return `\r` on the summary screen at the end.
- **Multiple choice (where more than one option may be picked) behaves differently:** digits and space *toggle* an option on or off, and **Enter also toggles rather than confirming**. Confirming means moving right with `\x1b[C` onto the Submit control and then pressing `\r`. So an implementation that simply appends `\r` to confirm will silently flip an option instead of submitting.
- **Free-text answer:** the digit after the last option opens an inline editor; then the UTF-8 text; then `\r`.
- The prompt does not respond to bracketed-paste framing at all — wrapped input produces cursor movement and no state change — so only the unframed write path can drive it.

# What I would like tested

1. **Exact byte sequences** for each of the four shapes above, single and multi-question.
2. **The multiple-choice confirm shape specifically.** Assert `\x1b[C` then `\r`, and assert that no code path appends a bare `\r` as a confirmation after a toggle. This is the case I am most worried about because it is invisible on a quick read.
3. **Property tests over generated inputs.** Does any input at all produce a trailing `\r` directly after a toggle? Does any input produce output when the answer's shape disagrees with the question's own multiple-choice flag (it should refuse instead)? Does any input produce output for a terminal kind the function is meant to decline (it only supports one CLI; another is explicitly out of scope because the key behaviour above was measured against this one and does not carry over)?
4. **UTF-8 handling** in the free-text path — multi-byte characters, emoji, embedded newlines.
5. **Boundary cases**: zero options, one option, more than nine options (does the digit encoding still make sense?), an option index out of range, an empty free-text string.

# Also, a smaller ordering question

In the neighbouring `answer.ts`, a set of preconditions is evaluated before this function's output is written out. I would like to know whether the evaluation and the write genuinely happen inside a single held lock, or whether they are two separate steps with a gap in between. A gap matters here because the prompt on screen can close during it, and these key presses take effect immediately with no undo. Just tell me which it is, and point at the lines.

# Constraints

- Test files under `C:/Users/khair/Code Projects/fork-superset-windows-arm64/tmp/` please. Do not modify production source.
- No git commands that change state — other people are working in this repo right now.
- Do not edit build files or `package.json`.
- Do not send any output to my actual running terminal sessions. This function is pure; test it in isolation.

# Output

The tests you wrote, their real output, and per problem: the exact file and line, what the function does, what the spec above says it should do, a concrete input that demonstrates the difference, and the fix. If everything matches, say so plainly and tell me what you covered.

content.text:
Codex delivered something the AI reviewers didn't — it *ran the crypto on both runtimes and compared bytes*, 149 properties. The compatibility news is good: every HKDF derivation, all four AAD forms, the 39-byte header offsets, nonce encoding, full AES-GCM ciphertexts and tags matched, and each runtime opened the other's envelopes. The earlier interop fixes held.

But it found **three critical AES-GCM nonce-reuse paths**, each demonstrated by an executed test rather than argued:

1. **Android re-pairing** clears and reinitialises the shared counter *before* replacing the paired-device record. Crash in that window and the old key and prefix stay authoritative with a rewound counter — it printed `oldCounter=1001, resumedCounter=1001, nonceRepeated=true`.
2. **Any state rollback repeats nonces on both runtimes** — VM snapshot, profile restore, power loss. Nothing anchors the key and prefix to the newest durable high-water mark, and the Android store doesn't fsync the containing directory while its comment claims losing the last reservation is safe. Losing that write-ahead mark is precisely what makes emitted counters reusable.
3. **Two bridge state owners can regress the high-water mark.** `start()` doesn't mark itself in progress early enough and `stop()` clears state before closing the old nonce source, so a stale source's later `close()` writes a *lower* value and the next source re-emits nonces already used.

Nonce reuse under AES-GCM isn't a degraded-security condition, it's a broken one — it permits plaintext recovery and tag forgery.

Its architectural objection is the real finding, and I agree with it: nonce, replay and revocation authority all live in independently rollbackable flat files with no transaction and no anti-rollback anchor. Two of the criticals and one high (a restored device index silently reversing revocation while the retained key still authorises terminal writes) are the same root cause wearing different hats.

Also worth noting: the one differential mismatch is Android accepting non-canonical base64url tails the bridge rejects — a small parser-differential that's exactly the kind of thing only byte-level testing finds.

Meanwhile I applied the three mechanical fork fixes and re-gated: markers now 87/87 with all five seam tokens registered (they existed only in comments before, so the merge-survival mechanism was decorative), and the frozen pathspec is now `companion*` — I proved it matches both the 18 directory files and a sibling `companion.ts`, closing the shadow bypass.

Noted on `message.send`: strengthening the guards rather than cutting it. That goes in the fix batch.

Three agents still out — `fable-journeys`, and the two Codex runs I've now stripped of all security vocabulary after two refusals each. I'll consolidate every finding into one fix pass before `/simplify`, rather than editing files the reviewers are still reading.

== J1 core loop — WORKS in code, end to end ==
Hook capture (pane-map-hook.ts embedded superset-notify.py) validates strictly, drops loud, retries dot-only on companion rejection. Sink custody single-owner (companion-question-sink.ts). Text never truncated at any of 3 layers (refuse-not-truncate, 262,144-char cap). Push: FCM data-only, android.priority=high runtime-asserted, 3-min delay counted in desktop-awake time, fire-time `isStillUnanswered` re-check. Phone posts full question (BigTextStyle) or honest "N questions · tap to answer". Watch gets NATIVE full-text copy via Data Layer (phone notification setLocalOnly), renders every line step-by-step, review screen, honest 4-state outcome. Injection: guards re-run per keystroke, lease, idempotent replay, no retry ever.

BREAK (HIGH, silent): phone POST_NOTIFICATIONS denied → questions silently never posted. app-phone .../notifications/CompanionNotifications.kt:67,111,169 (`canPost()` → return, Log.w only) + MainActivity.kt:58 (denial → Log.w). == J2 multi-question (59%) ==
Phone: N questions full text w/ ordinals; single-select-only auto-submits on last tap (matches desk byte semantics); multiSelect = checkboxes + explicit Submit + explanation. Watch: one question per step, "2 of 3" label, review screen listing all choices ("NOT ANSWERED — do not send" if gap), refuses multiSelect/free-text legibly ("Answer at the desk").

User fills all questions first, then refused. Honest but wasted effort. Fix: run shape classification inside unanswerableReason so phone/watch disable upfront.

Minor: watch QuestionStore is single-slot — a second question arriving replaces current + wipes in-progress selections (QuestionStore.kt onQuestion resets selections unless same-id answer pending). Deliberate design; mid-answer stomp possible.

== J3 answered at desk first ==
Happy path fine: PostToolUse hook → sink resolve → cancelPending; phone foreground sweep retracts + tells watch (SessionViewModel.kt:113-132); watch cancels notification, shows Resolved w/ provenance.

BREAK (MEDIUM): read-api.ts:898 discards `reconcile()`'s settled ids → when the PostToolUse hook dies (documented ARM64 failure mode), heartbeat reconcile settles the record but `push.cancelPending` never fires → already-SENT phone+watch notifications persist until phone next foregrounds. Fire-time re-check covers only unfired pushes. Fix: capture return, cancelPending per settled id.

Sheet open during desk answer: sheet is a snapshot (no live feed — events.ws deliberately ungranted in index.ts, code-deliberate but NOT on your deliberate list); user taps option → instant submit → 409 already_resolved → "Someone answered this first. Nothing was sent." No double-injection window: state check + guard-1 transcript + first-answer-wins all hold even with a dead hook. Late discovery = friction only. Also: push sent-record retention 15 min → later retractions silently no-op (sweep is sole backstop).

== J4 both devices ==
First lease wins; loser sees 409 "another device is answering this question" (answer.ts:1290-1298) — but `leaseHolderLabel` is always null, so refusal never names WHICH device. Watch copy excellent: "Phone is answering / Refused — not queued." Phone-local double-guard (LocalAnswerLease) covers watch-relay vs phone race. Legible; minor anonymity gripe.

== J5 unhappy paths — strongest area ==
ConnectionClassifier.kt: 530="Desktop asleep or off" vs 502="Desktop awake, Superset closed" DISTINCT; 403 two-variant (bridge-rejected vs Cloudflare-blocked by content-type); 401 unpaired vs clock-skew; DNS→Offline; TLS/Timeout/503-starting all separate. Watch renders every state as its own sentence (AnswerStateScreen.kt describeConnection, exhaustive-when so new states break compile). `delivery()` NEVER_SENT vs POSSIBLY_SENT → honest Failed-vs-Unconfirmed. Unconfirmed on both surfaces: no retry, "Check status" read only, known:false → "it was not sent". Watchdog fires only with live agents, pauses on lock. Gap (LOW): FCM/push-pipeline faults + notification-permission state have no phone Diagnostics row — "phone stopped buzzing" is undiagnosable from the phone.

== J6 first run — DAY-ONE BLOCKERS ==
BREAK (HIGH): desktop "Pair a device" UI does not exist. `companion.openPairing` tRPC mutation (packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/companion/companion.ts) has ZERO callers anywhere in the fork — no renderer surface. PairingScreen.kt:122 tells the user "open Superset and choose 'Pair a device'" → that button isn't there. First run dead-ends without dev tooling.
BREAK (HIGH, known): cloudflared service install deliberately not done (SETUP.md) → transport dead out of box.
Good: LAN hop clearly communicated ("same Wi-Fi for the next half a minute — never leaves your network"), malformed QR rejected locally with typed errors, camera-permission flow legible. Watch between install and first launch: WearableListenerService receives pushes, but pre-permission `areNotificationsEnabled()`=false → no buzz, and the in-app warning is unseen until first launch — one-time silent window.

1. Phone POST_NOTIFICATIONS denied → whole product silently mute (worst).

Everything else fails loud — capture drops warn, refusals render with codes, guard failures 4xx with prose.

== VERDICT ==
The loop itself is day-one usable and unusually honest: full text always, four outcome states never collapsed, no retry, no double-injection window found, error taxonomy tells the user which machine to poke. But day one literally cannot begin: no pairing button + no tunnel service = J6 blocks everything before J1 runs once.

SINGLE MOST-IMPROVING CHANGE: ship the desktop "Pair a device" surface (renderer entry → companion.openPairing → QR dialog). - The pairing URI contains a **256-bit pairing code in its URL fragment**. It MUST NOT be logged, written to disk, sent to any telemetry, or persisted in renderer state beyond the dialog's lifetime. - Do not render the code as selectable/copyable text. The QR is the transport; showing the raw secret invites a screenshot.
- The window is single-use and 120 seconds by design. Do not add a "keep it open" affordance.

## Fork constraints

- Put as much as possible in **fork-only files**. Every line added to an upstream-owned file is permanent merge burden.
- Add a **unique marker token** — use `(COMPANION-PAIRING-UI)` — as a literal comment in your new code, AND at each upstream-file seam you touch. Then register it in the `markers` block of `FEATURES.md`, tab-separated, pointing at a root that contains it. Follow the format of the existing rows exactly. If you touch more than one upstream file in different trees, mint a distinct token per seam and register each — a marker satisfied only by fork-only files cannot detect a merge deleting the seam that reaches them. That exact mistake was just found and fixed here, so do not repeat it.
- Also add a row to the FEATURES.md feature table describing the surface, matching the style of the neighbouring companion rows.
- Do NOT edit `package.json`, `bun.lock`, or any file under `packages/host-service/src/companion/`.

# Verify before reporting

- `node scripts/check-feature-markers.mjs` must pass and must include your new token(s).
- `node scripts/check-dangerous-diagnostics.mjs` must stay clean (this is the REFERR gate; it fails the nightly build).
- `bunx biome check <only the files you touched>` must be clean. **Never** run a root-level `bun run lint:fix` — it has previously EOL-rewritten 4,633 files in this repo.
- Type-check scoped to what you touched. The repo carries known pre-existing type debt in untouched files; distinguish that from anything you introduced.

# Rules

- Do NOT run any git command that changes state. Other agents are working in this repo concurrently.
- Do not modify files under `packages/host-service/src/companion/` — that directory is frozen and another pass is editing it.
- From the user's standing rules: validate at API boundaries; fail fast and loud; no defensive programming that masks failures; no sensible defaults for missing values; never catch an unexpected error just to hide it. Avoid `any`.
- Never print a secret value.

# Report

Files created and modified with full paths, the entry point you chose and why it fits the existing UI, how you rendered the QR, the marker tokens you registered and where, your real gate output, and anything you could not verify without running the desktop app.
